adrs.title: Backend Runtime — .NET 9 (STS)
adrs.verbatim:
## Context and Problem Statement

The EM2Devs.Todo backend needs a runtime that can deliver a modern API, support gamification workloads, and keep the development experience productive. The .NET ecosystem offers multiple active release tracks simultaneously, each with different feature sets and support timelines. Which .NET version should be used as the foundation for the backend?

## Decision Drivers

- Performance: throughput, latency, and memory efficiency for an API handling concurrent user requests
- Modern API patterns: minimal APIs, native AOT compilation, built-in OpenAPI generation
- Developer experience: reduced boilerplate, improved diagnostics, tooling quality
- Ecosystem maturity: NuGet package compatibility, third-party library support
- Support timeline: how long the version receives security patches and bug fixes
- Upgrade path: how straightforward it is to migrate to the next version when it becomes available

## Considered Options

- .NET 9 (STS — latest stable as of 2026-03)
- .NET 8 (LTS — long-term support, 3-year support window)
- .NET 10 (Preview — in active development, not yet GA)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: ".NET 9 (STS)", because it is the latest stable release and includes the most complete set of modern developer experience improvements (minimal APIs, native AOT, first-class OpenAPI generation via `Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi`, improved `System.Text.Json` performance and source generation). Its 18-month support window comfortably covers the project's development and initial production lifetime, and upgrading to .NET 10 LTS when it reaches GA is well-established as a low-friction process.

### Positive Consequences

- Access to all .NET 9 performance improvements (JIT, GC, LINQ, collections)
- Built-in OpenAPI document generation without third-party packages for baseline scenarios
- Native AOT support allows exploring cold-start optimisation for container deployments
- Improved `System.Text.Json` source generation reduces serialisation overhead
- Minimal API refinements (typed results, `IEndpointFilter`, `RouteGroupBuilder`) keep API code lean
- Straightforward upgrade path to .NET 10 LTS once GA

### Negative Consequences

- STS support ends ~May 2026; the team must plan a .NET 10 upgrade before end of support
- A small number of third-party packages may not yet have fully adopted .NET 9 target frameworks (mitigated by net8.0 compatibility)

### Neutral

- .NET 10 preview packages are installable alongside .NET 9, allowing early experimentation without committing to the preview runtime in production
- No change to existing .NET knowledge base — .NET 9 is fully backward-compatible with .NET 8 library patterns

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### .NET 9 (STS — latest stable)

The current stable release at project inception. Ships with minimal API improvements, native AOT hardening, built-in OpenAPI support, and the best-in-class performance numbers in the .NET series to date.

- Good, because all modern API patterns are available without workarounds
- Good, because built-in OpenAPI generation removes `Swashbuckle` / `NSwag` as a hard dependency for baseline documentation
- Good, because native AOT is production-stable, enabling leaner container images
- Good, because upgrade to .NET 10 is a well-trodden, low-risk path
- Bad, because 18-month STS window is shorter than .NET 8 LTS; requires a planned upgrade

### .NET 8 (LTS)

The previous major release with a 3-year LTS support window ending November 2026. Fully stable and widely adopted.

- Good, because 3-year LTS provides a longer support runway without forced upgrades
- Good, because maximum third-party package compatibility
- Bad, because misses DX improvements shipped in .NET 9 (OpenAPI generation, minimal API refinements, improved diagnostics)
- Bad, because using an older stable when a newer stable is available introduces unnecessary technical lag at project inception

### .NET 10 (Preview)

The next major release, in active development at time of decision. Not yet production-ready.

- Good, because would eventually be LTS with 3-year support
- Good, because allows building against future-facing APIs
- Bad, because preview releases carry breaking changes between preview drops
- Bad, because not suitable for production use; no support SLA
- Bad, because tooling and third-party package compatibility is incomplete during preview

## More Information

- [.NET release schedule and support policy](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/platform/support/policy/dotnet-core)
- [.NET 9 What's New](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/whats-new/dotnet-9/overview)
- [ASP.NET Core 9 What's New](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/release-notes/aspnetcore-9.0)

adrs.title: Frontend Framework — SvelteKit / Svelte 5
adrs.verbatim:
## Context and Problem Statement

EM2Devs.Todo is a gamified todo application that requires an interactive frontend with animations, real-time progress updates, achievement notifications, and a dashboard-style UI. The framework choice will determine the long-term developer experience, bundle size, and how naturally the gamification layer can be expressed in component code. Which frontend framework and meta-framework should be used?

## Decision Drivers

- Performance: runtime overhead, bundle size, and rendering efficiency matter for an interactive, animation-heavy UI
- Reactivity model: gamification state (XP, streaks, achievements) changes frequently and must propagate to the UI with minimal boilerplate
- Developer experience: how quickly can a developer write, understand, and maintain a component?
- Routing, SSR, and data loading: the meta-framework must handle these without bespoke configuration
- Ecosystem: availability of component libraries and integrations
- Bundle size: smaller output means faster initial load, especially on mobile networks

## Considered Options

- SvelteKit with Svelte 5 (runes reactivity model)
- Next.js with React (React 18 / 19, App Router)
- Nuxt with Vue 3 (Composition API)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "SvelteKit with Svelte 5", because Svelte compiles components to vanilla JavaScript at build time — there is no virtual DOM and no framework runtime shipped to the browser. This produces the leanest possible output for an interactive, gamified UI. Svelte 5's runes (`$state`, `$derived`, `$effect`) provide fine-grained, explicit reactivity that maps cleanly to gamification state (XP counters, streak timers, achievement progress). SvelteKit handles routing, SSR, data loading (`load` functions), and form actions with minimal ceremony.

### Positive Consequences

- No virtual DOM diffing overhead; animations and frequent state updates are cheap
- Compiled output is small — faster initial load and better Lighthouse scores
- Svelte 5 runes make reactive state explicit and easy to trace (no hidden proxies or compiler magic for component state)
- SvelteKit `load` functions co-locate data fetching with routes, reducing boilerplate
- Built-in transitions and animation primitives reduce reliance on additional animation libraries
- Straightforward TypeScript integration with full type safety in templates

### Negative Consequences

- Smaller component library ecosystem compared to React; developers may need to build more components from scratch or adapt headless libraries
- Svelte 5 runes are a significant syntax change from Svelte 4; team must familiarise themselves with the new model
- Fewer Svelte-specific hiring candidates compared to React; onboarding React-only developers requires a short learning curve

### Neutral

- SvelteKit supports both SSR and SPA/CSR modes per route; the gamification dashboard may ship as a CSR route while landing pages use SSR
- The Svelte ecosystem is growing rapidly; major UI libraries (shadcn-svelte, Melt UI) have adopted Svelte 5

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### SvelteKit with Svelte 5

A compiler-first framework that ships no runtime to the browser. Svelte 5 replaces the legacy reactive declarations with an explicit runes API.

- Good, because compiled output has minimal runtime overhead — ideal for animation-heavy gamified UIs
- Good, because runes (`$state`, `$derived`, `$effect`) provide clear, composable reactivity without context boilerplate
- Good, because SvelteKit covers routing, SSR, data loading, and API routes in one cohesive package
- Good, because built-in `animate:`, `transition:`, and `use:` directives handle most gamification animation needs natively
- Good, because bundle sizes are consistently smaller than equivalent React or Vue apps
- Bad, because component library ecosystem is smaller; some React-ecosystem libraries have no Svelte equivalent
- Bad, because Svelte 5 runes are still relatively new; community patterns and best practices are still stabilising

### Next.js with React

The dominant React meta-framework. App Router (introduced in Next.js 13) uses React Server Components for server-side rendering.

- Good, because React has the largest component library ecosystem (shadcn/ui, Radix, Headless UI, etc.)
- Good, because hiring pool of React developers is the largest of any frontend framework
- Good, because Next.js App Router is mature and production-proven at scale
- Bad, because React ships a runtime to the browser; bundle size is larger by default
- Bad, because React Server Components add conceptual complexity (server vs. client component boundaries) that requires careful management in an interactive app
- Bad, because frequent re-renders in complex gamification state require explicit memoisation (`useMemo`, `useCallback`, `React.memo`)

### Nuxt with Vue 3

Vue's official meta-framework. Vue 3 Composition API provides a clean reactivity model.

- Good, because Vue 3's `ref`/`reactive` Composition API is intuitive and well-documented
- Good, because Nuxt's auto-imports and conventions reduce boilerplate significantly
- Good, because strong ecosystem in Europe and Asia-Pacific; good hiring pool in those regions
- Bad, because Vue's component library ecosystem, while solid (Vuetify, PrimeVue), is smaller than React's
- Bad, because Vue ships a runtime; bundle size advantage over React is marginal compared to Svelte
- Bad, because the team has no existing Vue experience; learning curve is similar to Svelte without the bundle size benefit

## More Information

- [Svelte 5 Runes documentation](https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/what-are-runes)
- [SvelteKit documentation](https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/introduction)
- [Svelte 5 migration guide from Svelte 4](https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/v5-migration-guide)
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-013-frontend-state" status="accepted" title="Frontend State Management — Svelte 5 Runes + Stores + SvelteKit Load Functions" customLabel="ADR-013" /> — Frontend state management strategy

adrs.title: Database — PostgreSQL with JSONB
adrs.verbatim:
## Context and Problem Statement

EM2Devs.Todo needs to persist two broad categories of data: structured relational data (users, todo items, projects, due dates, completion status) and flexible, schema-evolving gamification data (achievement definitions, user progress snapshots, activity feeds, badge metadata, XP event logs). The challenge is that gamification schemas tend to evolve rapidly during product development while relational data benefits from strict type constraints and referential integrity. Which database strategy best serves both needs without excessive operational complexity?

## Decision Drivers

- Data integrity: relational data must have enforced constraints, foreign keys, and type safety
- Schema flexibility: gamification data structures will evolve frequently; migrations must not block iteration
- Query performance: the application must efficiently query both structured and semi-structured data in the same request
- Operational simplicity: minimise the number of distinct database systems to operate and monitor
- Ecosystem: quality of ORM/driver support in the .NET ecosystem
- Cost: self-hostable, with no per-row or per-operation pricing at the managed cloud tier

## Considered Options

- PostgreSQL (single database, JSONB for flexible columns)
- Polyglot persistence: MongoDB for gamification data + PostgreSQL for relational data
- SQL Server (managed on Azure)
- SQLite (embedded, for local/single-instance use)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "PostgreSQL with JSONB", because a single PostgreSQL instance covers both relational and document-style needs. JSONB columns provide indexed, queryable semi-structured storage for gamification payloads, delivering approximately 90% of what a dedicated document store would offer without the operational cost of running and synchronising two separate database systems. PostgreSQL's GIN indexes on JSONB enable efficient querying of nested gamification data. The .NET ecosystem has first-class support via EF Core with Npgsql.

### Positive Consequences

- Single database engine to operate, monitor, back up, and restore
- JSONB columns give gamification schemas room to evolve without blocking migrations on all related tables
- GIN indexes on JSONB allow targeted queries into achievement progress and activity feed entries
- Full ACID transactions span both relational and JSONB data — no cross-database consistency problems
- EF Core + Npgsql supports JSONB mapping with `UseJsonb()` on owned entity types
- PostgreSQL is open-source, freely hostable, and available as a managed service on every major cloud

### Negative Consequences

- JSONB queries are less ergonomic than a native document store API when deeply nested access is required
- Lack of schema enforcement on JSONB columns means the application layer must validate gamification payloads
- Large JSONB documents stored in hot tables can increase table bloat; requires periodic `VACUUM` tuning for high-write gamification event tables

### Neutral

- Schema migrations (via EF Core migrations or Flyway) apply to the relational columns; JSONB columns evolve through application-level versioning conventions
- If gamification data volume becomes extreme in the future, a dedicated time-series or document store can be introduced incrementally — the relational core stays in PostgreSQL

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### PostgreSQL with JSONB

A single relational database where flexible gamification data lives in indexed JSONB columns alongside strongly-typed relational tables.

- Good, because one database = one connection pool, one backup strategy, one monitoring target
- Good, because ACID transactions span structured and JSONB data — critical for consistent XP award + achievement unlock sequences
- Good, because GIN-indexed JSONB enables efficient queries into activity feeds and achievement progress without a full table scan
- Good, because Npgsql and EF Core provide strong .NET support, including LINQ-to-JSONB query translation
- Good, because open-source with no licensing cost; first-class managed offering on AWS (RDS), Azure (Flexible Server), GCP (Cloud SQL), and Supabase
- Bad, because deeply nested JSONB access is more verbose than a native document API
- Bad, because application layer must enforce schema consistency within JSONB columns

### Polyglot Persistence (MongoDB + PostgreSQL)

Use MongoDB Atlas or a self-hosted replica set for gamification documents and PostgreSQL for relational data.

- Good, because MongoDB's native document model and query language are purpose-built for nested, flexible schemas
- Good, because MongoDB Change Streams enable real-time gamification event propagation with no additional infrastructure
- Bad, because two databases double the operational surface: two connection pools, two backup strategies, two monitoring pipelines, two sets of cloud costs
- Bad, because cross-database transactions are not natively supported; distributed saga patterns add significant complexity to XP award + achievement unlock sequences
- Bad, because two ORMs/drivers must be maintained (.NET EF Core for PostgreSQL + MongoDB .NET Driver), increasing dependency surface
- Bad, because premature optimisation — JSONB is sufficient for the anticipated gamification data volumes at this stage

### SQL Server

Microsoft's relational database with JSON support via `JSON_VALUE`/`OPENJSON`.

- Good, because tight Azure integration and Azure SQL Managed Instance simplify managed hosting on Azure
- Good, because JSON functions cover basic semi-structured data needs
- Bad, because licensing costs (even on Azure) are higher than PostgreSQL at equivalent compute tiers
- Bad, because `JSON_VALUE` / `OPENJSON` are less capable than PostgreSQL JSONB (no GIN indexing equivalent; no native JSON type — stored as `nvarchar`)
- Bad, because less value delivered per dollar compared to PostgreSQL for this project's requirements

### SQLite

An embedded, serverless relational database suitable for local development and single-node deployments.

- Good, because zero operational overhead; the database is a file
- Good, because excellent for local development and integration tests
- Bad, because concurrent write throughput is limited by a single write-ahead log; not suitable for multi-user production workloads
- Bad, because JSONB equivalents are limited; JSON functions exist but lack indexing depth
- Bad, because no native network access; cannot be shared across multiple backend instances

## More Information

- [PostgreSQL JSONB documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html)
- [Npgsql EF Core provider — JSON/JSONB mapping](https://www.npgsql.org/efcore/mapping/json.html)
- [PostgreSQL GIN indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/gin-intro.html)

- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-020-db-migrations" status="accepted" title="Database Migrations — EF Core Migrations via CI/CD Pipeline" customLabel="ADR-020" /> — Database migration strategy

adrs.title: API Style — REST Minimal APIs + SignalR + Scalar API Docs
adrs.verbatim:
## Context and Problem Statement

EM2Devs.Todo needs an API layer that covers two distinct communication patterns: standard CRUD operations for todos, users, achievements, and quests; and real-time push of gamification events (XP awarded, achievement unlocked, leaderboard updated) to connected clients. A single protocol choice must cover both patterns, or a well-defined combination must be selected. What API style and tooling should back the EM2Devs.Todo backend?

## Decision Drivers

- Resource model clarity: todos, users, achievements, and quests map cleanly to discrete resources
- Real-time capability: gamification events must reach the client within seconds of the triggering domain event, without polling
- .NET 9 first-class support: prefer solutions that align with the investment direction of the .NET team
- OpenAPI generation and developer experience: API surface must be explorable and documented out of the box
- Frontend integration: the SvelteKit frontend needs both a typed HTTP client and a real-time event stream
- Scalability: the real-time layer must support horizontal scaling with a backplane

## Considered Options

- REST with .NET 9 Minimal APIs + SignalR + Scalar
- REST with ASP.NET Core Controllers + SignalR + Swagger UI
- GraphQL (Hot Chocolate) with subscriptions

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "REST with .NET 9 Minimal APIs + SignalR + Scalar", because it combines the leanest possible HTTP API surface for resource operations with a first-class real-time push channel, uses tooling that .NET 9 is directly investing in, and avoids framework overhead that is not justified by the resource model of this application.

The layers of the chosen approach are:

- **Minimal APIs** handle all CRUD endpoints. Route groups (`RouteGroupBuilder`) keep endpoint registration organised by feature. `TypedResults` make return types explicit and contribute to accurate OpenAPI schema generation.
- **SignalR Hub** (`GameHub`) receives domain events published from the CQRS pipeline — `TodoCompleted -> XpAwarded -> AchievementUnlocked` — and pushes them to the appropriate connected clients using groups (per-user and global leaderboard).
- **Redis backplane** (<AdrLink slug="20260305-008-caching" status="accepted" title="Caching — Redis via .NET Aspire" customLabel="ADR-008" />) is wired to SignalR from day one so that adding a second API instance does not break real-time delivery.
- **Scalar** replaces Swagger UI as the interactive API documentation explorer. .NET 9 ships `Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi` for document generation; Scalar provides the UI layer. It is actively recommended by Microsoft for .NET 9+ projects.

### Positive Consequences

- Minimal APIs reduce boilerplate per endpoint and make the API surface easy to read and navigate
- .NET 9 built-in OpenAPI generation (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi`) is maintained by the .NET team — no third-party Swashbuckle dependency needed
- Scalar provides a modern, interactive API explorer that is easier to use than Swagger UI and renders well on large schemas
- SignalR's hub model cleanly separates the real-time channel from the HTTP layer; clients subscribe to exactly the events they need
- The Redis backplane means horizontal scaling is possible without rearchitecting the real-time layer
- Route groups keep Minimal API registration organised as the surface grows

### Negative Consequences

- Two protocols (HTTP and WebSocket/SignalR) means the frontend must manage two connection types and their lifecycle independently
- SignalR adds a persistent connection overhead per active client; connection limits must be monitored as user count grows
- Scalar is newer than Swagger UI and has a smaller community surface, though it is well-maintained and backed by a dedicated team

### Neutral

- Minimal APIs and Controllers coexist in a .NET 9 project if legacy or third-party middleware requires controllers; this is not a binary lock-in
- SignalR falls back to long-polling transparently when WebSocket connections are unavailable (e.g., certain proxies), which maintains compatibility at the cost of some efficiency

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### REST with .NET 9 Minimal APIs + SignalR + Scalar

Lean HTTP endpoints for resource operations, a dedicated real-time hub for gamification events, and a modern documentation UI. All three are actively developed and aligned with .NET 9 investment priorities.

- Good, because Minimal APIs are the primary pattern the .NET team is investing in for .NET 9+
- Good, because `Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi` generates accurate OpenAPI documents without third-party packages
- Good, because SignalR is the mature, .NET-native real-time library with built-in fallback transports and backplane support
- Good, because Scalar is recommended by Microsoft for .NET 9 projects and provides a significantly better DX than Swagger UI
- Good, because route groups and endpoint filters keep API code organised without the controller ceremony
- Bad, because two protocols increase client complexity compared to a single protocol solution

### REST with ASP.NET Core Controllers + SignalR + Swagger UI

The traditional .NET API style. Well-understood and widely documented.

- Good, because controllers are familiar to developers with pre-.NET 6 experience
- Good, because attribute routing and action filters are well-documented and have broad ecosystem support
- Bad, because controllers introduce more ceremony (class per controller, constructor injection boilerplate) without adding capability for this use case
- Bad, because Swashbuckle (Swagger UI provider) is no longer actively maintained for .NET 9 and has been dropped from the default template
- Bad, because the .NET team's investment is clearly moving toward Minimal APIs; choosing controllers creates tech debt from inception

### GraphQL (Hot Chocolate) with Subscriptions

A single graph-based API where subscriptions replace SignalR for real-time events.

- Good, because a single protocol covers both query/mutation and real-time subscription patterns
- Good, because the type system and introspection offer strong self-documentation
- Good, because Hot Chocolate is a mature, actively developed GraphQL server for .NET
- Bad, because GraphQL's strengths (flexible field selection, nested queries) are not needed when the resource boundaries are clear and fixed
- Bad, because Hot Chocolate adds significant dependency weight and a new mental model for a team already fluent in REST
- Bad, because REST is more familiar to the anticipated frontend and mobile consumers; GraphQL requires a GraphQL-aware client
- Bad, because overkill for the current resource surface (todos, users, achievements, quests)

## More Information

- [ASP.NET Core Minimal APIs overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/overview)
- [Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi (.NET 9)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/openapi/overview)
- [Scalar .NET integration](https://github.com/scalar/scalar/blob/main/packages/scalar.aspnetcore/README.md)
- [ASP.NET Core SignalR overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/signalr/introduction)
- [SignalR Redis backplane](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/signalr/redis-backplane)
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-001-backend-runtime" status="accepted" title="Backend Runtime — .NET 9 (STS)" customLabel="ADR-001" /> — .NET 9 as the backend runtime
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-008-caching" status="accepted" title="Caching — Redis via .NET Aspire" customLabel="ADR-008" /> — Redis backplane for SignalR and caching

adrs.title: Orchestration — .NET Aspire
adrs.verbatim:
## Context and Problem Statement

EM2Devs.Todo is a multi-service system: a .NET API backend, a SvelteKit frontend, a PostgreSQL database, and (later) a Redis cache and background worker. During development, starting all services consistently, wiring up connection strings, and having visibility into distributed traces and health is a significant source of friction. In production, the same services need container images and deployment manifests. What tooling should orchestrate services locally and generate deployment artifacts?

## Decision Drivers

- Local developer experience: a new team member should be able to start the entire stack with a single command
- Observability out of the box: distributed traces, structured logs, and health check dashboards without bespoke configuration
- Service discovery: services must resolve each other's addresses without hardcoded ports in every developer's config file
- Deployment artifact generation: local orchestration tooling should produce container-ready artifacts (Docker Compose, Kubernetes manifests, Azure Container Apps bicep) without manual authoring
- Multi-service orchestration: must handle .NET services and non-.NET services (SvelteKit, PostgreSQL container, Redis container)
- Resilience defaults: standard HTTP retry policies and circuit breakers should be available to all services without per-service boilerplate

## Considered Options

- .NET Aspire (AppHost + ServiceDefaults)
- Docker Compose only
- Manual setup (separate terminal tabs, environment files, no shared tooling)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: ".NET Aspire", because it solves the local multi-service orchestration problem with minimal configuration while simultaneously producing cloud-ready deployment artifacts. The `AppHost` project becomes the single entry point — running it starts the API, the SvelteKit frontend (as an executable resource), PostgreSQL (as a container resource), and Redis. Aspire injects connection strings and service URLs via environment variables, eliminating per-developer `.env` juggling. `ServiceDefaults` wires OpenTelemetry, health checks, and Polly resilience policies into every .NET service automatically. The Aspire dashboard provides real-time traces, logs, and metrics during development without any additional infrastructure.

Aspire is a development-time and build-time tool — it does not run in production. It produces container images and deployment manifests (Docker Compose, Kubernetes, Azure Container Apps via `azd`) that run on any container platform.

### Positive Consequences

- Single `dotnet run --project AppHost` starts the entire stack; no manual service coordination
- OpenTelemetry traces span the API and worker automatically via `ServiceDefaults`; traces are visible in the Aspire dashboard immediately
- Health check endpoints are registered on all .NET services via `ServiceDefaults` with no per-service code
- Polly retry and circuit-breaker policies are available to all services via `AddServiceDefaults()` with sensible defaults
- `azd` integration generates Azure Container Apps deployment with one command when the cloud target is decided
- Non-.NET services (SvelteKit, PostgreSQL, Redis) are orchestrated as first-class resources alongside .NET services
- Connection strings and service URLs are injected at runtime; no hardcoded ports or connection strings in source control

### Negative Consequences

- Aspire AppHost is an additional project in the solution; new contributors must understand its role
- Aspire's component packages (e.g., `Aspire.Hosting.PostgreSQL`) pin compatible container image versions; teams must update these when upgrading infrastructure versions
- The Aspire dashboard is only available during local development; production observability requires a separate backend (see <AdrLink slug="20260305-012-observability" status="accepted" title="Observability — Grafana Stack + Serilog + Aspire Dashboard" customLabel="ADR-012" />)

### Neutral

- Aspire does not prescribe a production hosting platform; it generates artifacts for multiple targets (Docker Compose, ACA, Kubernetes)
- The AppHost project is a .NET console app and can be version-controlled, code-reviewed, and tested like any other project

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### .NET Aspire (AppHost + ServiceDefaults)

A developer-focused orchestration framework from Microsoft that combines a fluent `AppHost` API with a `ServiceDefaults` extension package and a local dashboard.

- Good, because one F5 (or `dotnet run`) starts all services with correct environment wiring
- Good, because OpenTelemetry, health checks, and Polly resilience are pre-configured for all .NET services via `AddServiceDefaults()`
- Good, because the local dashboard provides distributed traces, structured logs, and environment variable inspection with no additional setup
- Good, because `azd` integration generates Azure Container Apps deployment manifests directly from the AppHost graph
- Good, because non-.NET workloads (SvelteKit, databases, caches) integrate as container or executable resources
- Good, because connection strings are injected via environment variables; no secrets committed to source control
- Bad, because introduces an additional project (`AppHost`) that developers must understand
- Bad, because Aspire is a Microsoft-first tool; deepest integration is with Azure, though Docker Compose output works for any platform

### Docker Compose Only

A YAML-based multi-container definition used to start and link services locally.

- Good, because Docker Compose is universal — works with any language, framework, or cloud provider
- Good, because no additional tooling or SDK dependency beyond Docker Desktop
- Bad, because no built-in observability; developers must manually add OpenTelemetry collector, Jaeger, or similar
- Bad, because service discovery relies on Docker network aliases; local port mapping and `appsettings` overrides must be maintained manually
- Bad, because no deployment artifact generation beyond the Compose file itself; Kubernetes or ACA manifests must be authored separately
- Bad, because resilience policies (retries, circuit breakers) require explicit per-service configuration with no shared defaults

### Manual Setup

Each service started independently via separate terminal processes, with connection strings configured per-developer via `.env` files or `appsettings.Development.json`.

- Good, because no tooling dependency; works in any environment
- Bad, because onboarding is slow — new developers must discover and configure each service independently
- Bad, because port conflicts, incorrect connection strings, and stale environment variables are common failure modes
- Bad, because no shared observability; debugging distributed flows requires correlating disparate log streams manually
- Bad, because generating deployment artifacts is entirely manual

## More Information

- [.NET Aspire documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/aspire/get-started/aspire-overview)
- [.NET Aspire ServiceDefaults](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/aspire/fundamentals/service-defaults)
- [Aspire + Azure Developer CLI (azd)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/developer/azure-developer-cli/azure-developer-cli-vs-aspire)

adrs.title: Hosting — Containers (Deployment Target TBD)
adrs.verbatim:
## Context and Problem Statement

EM2Devs.Todo is in active development. The team needs to decide on a hosting and deployment strategy, but the production cloud target has not yet been chosen. Committing to a specific cloud platform now (Azure App Service, AWS ECS, etc.) risks incurring lock-in costs before requirements — budget, region preferences, existing agreements — are fully understood. At the same time, the project needs a clear path from local development to a production-grade deployment. What hosting strategy allows the team to build confidently without premature cloud lock-in?

## Decision Drivers

- Platform agnosticism: avoid hard dependencies on a single cloud provider's proprietary APIs during development
- Aspire compatibility: the deployment strategy must align with what Aspire generates from the AppHost definition
- Production readiness path: there must be a clear and credible route to production without a major re-architecture
- Cost flexibility: the team should be free to choose the most cost-effective platform when the time comes
- Operational consistency: the same artifact (container image) that runs locally should run in production

## Considered Options

- Containers (Docker) with cloud target deferred
- Azure (App Service or Container Apps)
- AWS (ECS / Fargate)
- Self-hosted (VPS or bare metal)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Containers with deployment target TBD", because containerising every service (API, worker, frontend) provides a portable, cloud-agnostic artifact that can be deployed to any container platform. Aspire's `AppHost` already models the system as a set of container resources; `azd` can generate Azure Container Apps manifests, and the same AppHost graph can produce a Docker Compose file for any other platform. Deferring the cloud target decision is rational: the work required to switch targets is minimal when the deployment unit is a container image, and the team gains concrete operational experience before committing to a vendor.

When production deployment is imminent, the cloud target will be chosen based on cost, team familiarity, and feature requirements, and a follow-up ADR will record that decision (see "More Information" below).

### Positive Consequences

- Container images run identically in local Aspire orchestration, CI pipelines, and production — no environment-specific surprises
- No cloud-provider SDK calls in application code; switching targets requires only infrastructure changes
- Aspire-generated Docker Compose file is a complete, runnable deployment descriptor for any Docker-capable host
- Azure Container Apps remains the default first-candidate production target due to first-class Aspire/`azd` support, but is not binding
- CI pipeline can build and push images to any registry (GitHub Container Registry, ECR, ACR) without re-work

### Negative Consequences

- Without a fixed cloud target, environment-specific configuration (IAM roles, managed identity, secrets management integration) cannot be fully designed yet; these remain TBD
- Deferring the cloud target means some infrastructure-as-code work will need to be done closer to production deployment
- Self-hosting is a viable option but would require the team to manage container orchestration (Docker Swarm or Kubernetes) — adding operational burden

### Neutral

- The decision to defer does not prevent the team from prototyping on a preferred cloud target during development
- This ADR will be superseded by a follow-up hosting decision ADR once the production target is confirmed

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Containers (Docker) with Target TBD

Build container images for all services. Defer selection of the production runtime (cloud provider and service tier) until closer to deployment.

- Good, because portable artifact — one image works on any container platform
- Good, because aligns directly with what Aspire generates; no translation layer needed
- Good, because CI/CD pipeline can be built and tested before the cloud target is chosen
- Good, because cost and feature comparisons can be made with a working system rather than estimates
- Bad, because infrastructure-as-code (IaC), secrets management, and networking decisions are deferred; they must be addressed before go-live

### Azure (App Service / Container Apps)

Deploy directly to Azure, using App Service for the API and Static Web Apps for the SvelteKit frontend, or Azure Container Apps for a unified container-based deployment.

- Good, because Azure Container Apps has first-class Aspire support via `azd`; `azd up` can deploy the entire Aspire-defined topology
- Good, because managed identity, Key Vault, and Azure Monitor integration simplify secrets and observability configuration
- Good, because Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server is a mature managed offering
- Bad, because committing to Azure now forecloses cost comparisons; Azure is not always the cheapest option for small workloads
- Bad, because proprietary integrations (managed identity, Azure Monitor SDK) would create lock-in if introduced too early

### AWS (ECS / Fargate)

Deploy container images to Amazon ECS using Fargate for serverless container compute.

- Good, because Fargate eliminates EC2 instance management; pay-per-task pricing suits variable workloads
- Good, because AWS has the largest global infrastructure footprint and mature container tooling
- Bad, because Aspire does not have a native `azd`-equivalent for ECS; Terraform or CDK IaC must be authored manually
- Bad, because AWS RDS PostgreSQL and Fargate costs can exceed Azure equivalents at small scales

### Self-Hosted (VPS or Bare Metal)

Run containers on a rented VPS (Hetzner, DigitalOcean) using Docker Compose or a lightweight Kubernetes distribution (k3s).

- Good, because lowest infrastructure cost at small scale; predictable monthly pricing
- Good, because full control over the environment; no cloud provider constraints
- Bad, because the team must manage OS updates, TLS certificates, backups, and container orchestration
- Bad, because scaling beyond a single node requires Kubernetes expertise that adds significant operational overhead

## More Information

- [Azure Container Apps + .NET Aspire (azd)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/developer/azure-developer-cli/azure-developer-cli-vs-aspire)
- [Docker documentation — multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-005-orchestration" status="accepted" title="Orchestration — .NET Aspire" customLabel="ADR-005" /> — .NET Aspire generates container images and deployment manifests

> **TBD:** A follow-up ADR must be created to record the final production hosting target (cloud provider, service tier, region) once the team is ready to deploy. This ADR will be marked as Superseded at that time.

adrs.title: Authentication — Auth0 with Social Logins
adrs.verbatim:
## Context and Problem Statement

EM2Devs.Todo is a gamified productivity app where user motivation is the core product. Friction at the signup gate directly undermines that motivation — a user who abandons registration never earns their first XP. The app must allow any new user to be authenticated and playing within seconds, using an account they already have, with no password to create or forget. At the same time, the backend needs a stable local user identity to attach todos, XP totals, achievements, and quest progress to. How should authentication and user identity be handled to satisfy both zero-friction onboarding and reliable backend-side user records?

## Decision Drivers

- Frictionless onboarding: users must be able to sign in with one click using an existing social account — no registration form, no password creation
- Social provider coverage: Apple, Google, Microsoft, and Meta are required at launch; additional providers should be addable without code changes to the backend
- Password-less by default: storing and managing passwords introduces credential risk and operational overhead that is not justified for this app
- MFA support: Auth0's built-in MFA satisfies security requirements without custom implementation
- Free tier generosity: the solution must be cost-free through early adoption (target: 25 000 MAU threshold)
- Developer experience: social OAuth2 flows are complex to implement correctly from scratch; a managed service removes that risk
- Local user record: the backend must maintain its own user entity (internal ID, display name, email, avatar URL, linked provider ID) that domain logic can reference — the identity provider is not the source of truth for application data

## Considered Options

- Auth0 (managed identity provider with social login support)
- Keycloak (self-hosted open-source identity provider)
- ASP.NET Identity + manual OAuth2 (self-managed social login flows)
- Entra ID / Azure AD (Microsoft managed identity platform)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Auth0 with social logins", because it delivers all required social providers out of the box, is free for the first 25 000 MAU, and requires roughly five minutes of configuration to wire up Apple, Google, Microsoft, and Meta — work that would take weeks to replicate safely in a self-managed solution. The approach preserves a clean separation of concerns: Auth0 handles credential verification and token issuance, while the backend maintains its own user record for all application domain data.

The sign-in flow is:

1. User taps "Sign in with Google" in the Flutter or SvelteKit client.
2. The client redirects to the Auth0-hosted login page, which proxies to Google's OAuth2 consent screen.
3. Google authenticates the user and returns an ID token (email, name, avatar URL) to Auth0.
4. Auth0 issues a token to the client, which forwards it to the EM2Devs.Todo backend.
5. The backend validates the token against Auth0's JWKS endpoint.
6. The backend checks whether a local `User` record already exists for the provider + provider user ID combination.
   - If no record exists: one is auto-created (internal UUID, display name from the social profile, email, avatar URL, linked provider ID). No form, no password, no manual step.
   - If a record exists: the user is logged in.
7. The backend issues its own short-lived JWT (<AdrLink slug="20260305-004-api-style" status="accepted" title="API Style — REST Minimal APIs + SignalR + Scalar API Docs" customLabel="ADR-004" />) for all subsequent API calls. Auth0 is not consulted again until the session expires.

The local `User` entity is essential — it is the root aggregate that todos, XP, achievements, and quest progress attach to. Auth0 owns the credential; the backend owns the application identity.

### Positive Consequences

- Any new user is authenticated and inside the app in under ten seconds, with no form to fill
- All required social providers (Apple, Google, Microsoft, Meta) are available through Auth0's connection library without writing OAuth2 flows
- Adding a new social provider (e.g., GitHub, LinkedIn) requires one Auth0 configuration change and no backend code changes
- Built-in MFA satisfies the security baseline (<AdrLink slug="20260305-021-security-baseline" status="accepted" title="Security Baseline — CORS, Rate Limiting, HTTPS, Input Validation, Security Headers" customLabel="ADR-021" />) without custom implementation
- The backend JWT layer means downstream services never call Auth0 on the hot path — Auth0 is only touched at login
- Auth0 free tier (25 000 MAU) covers the expected user base through early production

### Negative Consequences

- Auth0 is a third-party dependency; an outage or pricing change affects the login flow (mitigated by the backend's own JWT layer, which keeps authenticated sessions alive without re-hitting Auth0)
- If the Auth0 free tier is exceeded, costs scale per MAU — the team must plan for this threshold as a growth milestone
- Account linking across providers (e.g., a user who signs in with Google and later wants to use Apple) requires explicit handling; Auth0 supports it but the backend must also reconcile local records

### Neutral

- The backend JWT can be issued with any claims needed for authorisation (user ID, roles, feature flags), keeping the API layer independent of Auth0's token format
- Social profile data (avatar URL, display name) is captured at first login and stored locally; it is not re-fetched from the provider on every request
- Auth0's Universal Login page is hosted and managed by Auth0, which means it can be styled to match the app brand but is subject to Auth0's rendering constraints

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Auth0 (managed identity provider)

Auth0 is a cloud-hosted identity platform that manages the full OAuth2/OIDC flow for social providers. The developer configures connections (Google, Apple, etc.) in the Auth0 dashboard; Auth0 handles the redirect dance, token exchange, and user storage. The backend validates Auth0-issued tokens and syncs a local user record.

- Good, because all major social providers are pre-built connections requiring only a dashboard toggle
- Good, because 25 000 MAU are free — sufficient for launch and early growth without billing concern
- Good, because MFA, anomaly detection, and bot protection are available without additional code
- Good, because JWKS-based token validation is straightforward to implement in ASP.NET Core with `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer`
- Good, because the hosted login UI removes the need to build and maintain a login screen
- Bad, because it introduces a vendor dependency for the login path; Auth0 outages affect sign-in (not authenticated sessions)
- Bad, because exceeding the free tier introduces per-MAU costs that must be budgeted as the app grows

### Keycloak (self-hosted)

Keycloak is an open-source identity provider that can be hosted on the team's own infrastructure. It supports social login adapters and issues standard OIDC tokens.

- Good, because self-hosted — no vendor dependency, no per-MAU costs at scale
- Good, because open-source with a large community and extensive documentation
- Bad, because the team must provision, operate, and secure a Keycloak instance (or cluster), adding significant DevOps overhead at project inception
- Bad, because social login adapters require more configuration than Auth0's built-in connections
- Bad, because the operational burden is not justified when Auth0 is free within the target MAU range

### ASP.NET Identity + Manual OAuth2

Implement user management with ASP.NET Core Identity and manually implement OAuth2 authorization code flows for each social provider using a library such as `AspNet.Security.OAuth.Providers`.

- Good, because full ownership of the identity stack — no third-party dependency
- Good, because maximum flexibility in user data modelling and token format
- Bad, because implementing OAuth2 flows correctly (PKCE, state parameter, token refresh, error handling) is complex and error-prone
- Bad, because each social provider must be individually configured and tested; adding a new provider requires code changes
- Bad, because password management, credential storage, and breach response become team responsibilities
- Bad, because development time spent on auth plumbing is time not spent on gamification features

### Entra ID / Azure AD

Microsoft's managed identity platform, offering social login via B2C or External Identities and tight integration with the Microsoft ecosystem.

- Good, because first-class support for Microsoft (and GitHub, via enterprise directory) accounts
- Good, because deeply integrated with Azure services if Azure is the deployment target
- Bad, because configuring non-Microsoft social providers (Apple, Meta) in Entra is significantly more complex than in Auth0
- Bad, because Entra ID B2C pricing and setup complexity is higher than Auth0 for the initial use case
- Bad, because the mental model (tenants, policies, user flows) adds overhead compared to Auth0's simpler configuration surface

## More Information

- [Auth0 social connections documentation](https://auth0.com/docs/authenticate/identity-providers/social-identity-providers)
- [Auth0 pricing (free tier: 25 000 MAU)](https://auth0.com/pricing)
- [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer (.NET 9)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authentication/jwt-authn)
- [Sign In with Apple requirements for apps](https://developer.apple.com/sign-in-with-apple/get-started/)
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-004-api-style" status="accepted" title="API Style — REST Minimal APIs + SignalR + Scalar API Docs" customLabel="ADR-004" /> — JWT used for backend API authentication after the Auth0 login flow
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-021-security-baseline" status="accepted" title="Security Baseline — CORS, Rate Limiting, HTTPS, Input Validation, Security Headers" customLabel="ADR-021" /> — Security baseline (CORS, rate limiting, HTTPS, security headers)

adrs.title: Caching — Redis via .NET Aspire
adrs.verbatim:
## Context and Problem Statement

EM2Devs.Todo includes several categories of read-heavy data that are expensive to recompute on every request: leaderboards aggregate XP across all users, user profiles are fetched on every authenticated API call, and achievement definitions are a fixed catalogue read frequently but updated rarely. Beyond HTTP caching, the app uses SignalR (<AdrLink slug="20260305-004-api-style" status="accepted" title="API Style — REST Minimal APIs + SignalR + Scalar API Docs" customLabel="ADR-004" />) for real-time gamification event delivery. When the API runs as more than one instance — whether for load distribution or fault tolerance — SignalR requires a shared message backplane so that a client connected to instance A receives events published by instance B. What caching solution should be used to satisfy both the read-performance and the real-time backplane requirements?

## Decision Drivers

- Performance for read-heavy queries: leaderboards are computed from aggregate data across the full user table; recomputing on every request is not viable at scale
- Cache invalidation control: the team needs explicit, targeted invalidation (e.g., invalidate the leaderboard cache when any user's XP changes), not just TTL expiry
- SignalR backplane: multi-instance deployments require a pub/sub-capable backplane so SignalR messages are fanned out across all instances
- .NET Aspire integration: the project uses Aspire (<AdrLink slug="20260305-005-orchestration" status="accepted" title="Orchestration — .NET Aspire" customLabel="ADR-005" />) for local orchestration; the caching layer should integrate cleanly with the Aspire component model
- Operational simplicity: developers should not need to install and configure a cache server manually; local dev must work out of the box
- Versatility: a single solution should cover both caching and pub/sub to avoid running two separate infrastructure components

## Considered Options

- Redis via Aspire first-party component (`Aspire.StackExchange.Redis`)
- In-memory cache (`IMemoryCache` / `IDistributedCache` with in-memory provider)
- Memcached
- No caching (optimise queries instead)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Redis via .NET Aspire", because Redis is the only option that satisfies both the distributed caching and SignalR backplane requirements with a single component, and the first-party Aspire integration (`Aspire.StackExchange.Redis`) makes it automatically available during local development without any manual setup.

Redis is used for the following purposes in EM2Devs.Todo:

- **Leaderboard caching**: leaderboard queries (top-N users by XP, weekly/monthly aggregations) are computed and cached in Redis with explicit invalidation when a `XpAwarded` domain event is raised. Cache-aside pattern: check Redis first; on miss, compute from the database and populate the cache.
- **User profile caching**: the authenticated user's profile (display name, avatar, XP total, level, active quest) is cached per user ID. Invalidated on profile update or XP award.
- **Achievement definitions**: the achievement catalogue is a static-ish dataset loaded into Redis at startup and refreshed infrequently (or on admin update). Read path checks Redis; admin writes invalidate the entry.
- **SignalR backplane**: `AddStackExchangeRedis` is called on the SignalR service registration. All `GameHub` messages published by any API instance are fanned out via Redis pub/sub to all other instances, ensuring every connected client receives real-time gamification events regardless of which instance they are connected to.

During local development, Aspire provisions a Redis container automatically as part of the app host. No manual Docker command or local Redis installation is required.

### Positive Consequences

- Leaderboard response times drop significantly: a cache hit returns pre-computed data in sub-millisecond time vs. an aggregation query over the full user table
- SignalR works correctly in multi-instance deployments from day one — no future rearchitecting required when scaling horizontally
- Aspire's container provisioning means every developer has the same Redis version and configuration without manual setup steps
- `Aspire.StackExchange.Redis` registers `IConnectionMultiplexer` in the DI container with health checks, metrics, and tracing wired up automatically
- Redis's rich data structures (sorted sets, hashes) open the option to store leaderboard data natively in Redis rather than computing it from the relational database
- A single Redis instance serves both caching and pub/sub — one infrastructure component to operate

### Negative Consequences

- Redis is a network dependency during local development; if Aspire fails to start the container (e.g., Docker daemon not running), the app cannot start without a fallback
- Redis introduces a new operational component in production; the team must provision, monitor, and back up a Redis instance (or use a managed service such as Azure Cache for Redis)
- Cache invalidation logic must be maintained: as new domain events are added, developers must remember to invalidate relevant cache entries or accept stale data

### Neutral

- `StackExchange.Redis` is the de facto .NET Redis client; the Aspire component wraps it with minimal additional abstraction, so existing `StackExchange.Redis` documentation and patterns apply directly
- Redis persistence (RDB/AOF) is available but not required for cache use cases; if Redis is restarted, the cache is cold and warms up on first request
- Aspire supports both a local container and an existing external Redis connection string, making the transition from local dev to production straightforward

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Redis via .NET Aspire (`Aspire.StackExchange.Redis`)

A battle-tested distributed cache and pub/sub broker, integrated into the project via the first-party Aspire component. Aspire handles container lifecycle in local dev; production targets a managed Redis service.

- Good, because Redis is the industry-standard solution for distributed caching and pub/sub — abundant documentation, tooling, and operational patterns
- Good, because it is the only option that also satisfies the SignalR backplane requirement without adding a second infrastructure component
- Good, because `Aspire.StackExchange.Redis` wires up health checks, OpenTelemetry tracing, and metrics automatically
- Good, because Aspire provisions the Redis container during local dev — zero manual setup
- Good, because sorted sets make it possible to maintain a live leaderboard natively in Redis if the relational aggregate approach becomes too slow
- Bad, because Docker must be running locally for Aspire to start the Redis container
- Bad, because adds a managed Redis service cost in production (though Azure Cache for Redis Basic tier is inexpensive for early-stage use)

### In-Memory Cache (`IMemoryCache` / `IDistributedCache` in-memory)

The built-in .NET in-process cache. No external dependency; data lives in the process heap.

- Good, because zero infrastructure — no container, no external service, no Docker required
- Good, because trivial to set up (`services.AddMemoryCache()`)
- Good, because the fastest possible read path — data is already in process memory
- Bad, because not shared across instances — each API instance has its own isolated cache, leading to inconsistent reads and duplicate computation when scaled horizontally
- Bad, because cache is lost on every process restart
- Bad, because cannot be used as a SignalR backplane — disqualifying for the multi-instance requirement
- Bad, because memory pressure in the API process increases as cached datasets grow

### Memcached

A high-performance distributed memory cache designed for simple key-value workloads.

- Good, because extremely fast for pure key-value get/set operations
- Good, because well-understood operationally with managed hosting options
- Bad, because no pub/sub capability — cannot serve as a SignalR backplane, requiring a second broker (RabbitMQ, Redis) anyway
- Bad, because no first-party Aspire component; integration requires manual configuration
- Bad, because limited data structure support compared to Redis (no sorted sets, no hashes), restricting future optimisation options
- Bad, because solving both the caching and backplane requirements would require two separate infrastructure components instead of one

### No Caching (Optimise Queries Instead)

Rely entirely on database query optimisation, indexing, and connection pooling to deliver acceptable response times without an external cache.

- Good, because removes all cache invalidation complexity — data is always fresh from the source
- Good, because simpler architecture — fewer moving parts to operate and monitor
- Bad, because leaderboard queries aggregate XP across all users; with even a few thousand users this becomes a full-table aggregation that cannot be optimised away with indexes alone
- Bad, because does not address the SignalR multi-instance problem — a backplane is still required regardless of caching decisions
- Bad, because under load, repeated expensive queries will stress the database and degrade overall response times across all endpoints

## More Information

- [Aspire.StackExchange.Redis component documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/aspire/caching/stackexchange-redis-component)
- [SignalR Redis backplane (ASP.NET Core)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/signalr/redis-backplane)
- [StackExchange.Redis documentation](https://stackexchange.github.io/StackExchange.Redis/)
- [Azure Cache for Redis pricing](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/cache/)
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-004-api-style" status="accepted" title="API Style — REST Minimal APIs + SignalR + Scalar API Docs" customLabel="ADR-004" /> — SignalR for real-time gamification event delivery; Redis backplane referenced here
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-005-orchestration" status="accepted" title="Orchestration — .NET Aspire" customLabel="ADR-005" /> — .NET Aspire for service orchestration and local dev container provisioning

adrs.title: Data Access — EF Core (writes) + Dapper (reads)
adrs.verbatim:
## Context and Problem Statement

With CQRS separating the command (write) path from the query (read) path, the data access layer can be optimised independently for each concern. The command side handles domain-rich writes — entity creation, state transitions, aggregate persistence — where change tracking, domain modelling, and schema migration support are valuable. The query side handles read-optimised projections — leaderboards, dashboards, achievement summaries — where raw SQL performance and minimal overhead matter more than ORM convenience. Which data access approach should be used for each path?

## Decision Drivers

- CQRS alignment: data access strategy should mirror the command/query split
- Write-side domain modelling: support for change tracking, value objects, owned entities, and relationships
- Read-side performance: ability to write hand-crafted SQL for complex projections without ORM translation overhead
- Migration support: schema evolution must be tracked, auditable, and automatable
- Developer experience: familiar .NET tooling, strong IDE support, good documentation
- Dependency footprint: prefer established, well-maintained libraries without restrictive licensing

## Considered Options

- EF Core only
- Dapper only
- EF Core (writes) + Dapper (reads)
- Marten (document DB on PostgreSQL)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "EF Core (writes) + Dapper (reads)", because each tool is used where it provides the greatest benefit. EF Core handles the command path with full domain modelling, change tracking, relationship navigation, and migration management. Dapper handles the query path with raw SQL, minimal overhead, and direct result mapping — which is critical for complex read projections such as leaderboards and achievement summaries. This is a well-established pattern in .NET CQRS applications.

### Positive Consequences

- Commands retain full EF Core capabilities: change tracking, value objects, owned entities, `SaveChanges` unit of work
- Queries can use raw SQL tuned for read performance — no ORM query translation surprises
- EF Core Migrations provides a single, auditable schema history tracked in `__EFMigrationsHistory`
- Both libraries are battle-tested, open-source, and have strong .NET community support
- Clear architectural boundary: any file in a `Queries/` handler that touches the DB uses Dapper; any `Commands/` handler uses EF Core
- Dapper's lightweight mapping makes it straightforward to project directly into read model DTOs without domain entity overhead

### Negative Consequences

- Developers must understand and respect the boundary — EF Core must not be used for read projections that can be served by Dapper
- Two mental models for SQL interaction (LINQ vs raw SQL) require discipline to keep consistent
- Dapper does not participate in EF Core's Unit of Work; queries must use a separate `IDbConnection`

### Neutral

- Both EF Core and Dapper operate over the same PostgreSQL connection string — no additional infrastructure is introduced
- The boundary between EF Core and Dapper roughly maps to the command/query boundary already established by CQRS, keeping the rule easy to remember and enforce in code review

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### EF Core only

A single ORM for both commands and queries. EF Core's LINQ provider is used for all database interactions, with raw SQL as an escape hatch via `FromSqlRaw` when needed.

- Good, because a single library reduces cognitive load and keeps the data access model uniform
- Good, because change tracking, relationships, and migrations are all in one place
- Good, because strong IDE support for LINQ queries
- Bad, because EF Core query translation can generate suboptimal SQL for complex projections (leaderboards, multi-table aggregates) that are much easier to express and tune as raw SQL
- Bad, because the ORM abstraction adds overhead on the read path where it provides no write-side benefits

### Dapper only

Use Dapper's lightweight SQL mapping for all database interactions, writing raw SQL for both commands and queries.

- Good, because raw SQL gives complete control over query shape and performance on both paths
- Good, because zero ORM overhead across the board
- Bad, because no change tracking means domain-level state management must be implemented manually
- Bad, because no migration tooling — schema evolution requires a separate migration framework
- Bad, because complex domain relationships and value objects require manual mapping boilerplate

### EF Core (writes) + Dapper (reads)

Use EF Core on the command path for domain modelling and migrations, and Dapper on the query path for raw SQL projections.

- Good, because each tool is applied where it is strongest
- Good, because write-side retains full EF Core domain modelling and change tracking
- Good, because read-side projections are fast, explicit, and not subject to ORM translation quirks
- Good, because well-established pattern with strong community precedent in .NET CQRS applications
- Bad, because two data access libraries increase the initial setup surface area
- Bad, because the boundary between EF Core and Dapper must be actively maintained via team convention and code review

### Marten (document DB on PostgreSQL)

Use Marten as a document database and event store abstraction on top of PostgreSQL, replacing both EF Core and Dapper.

- Good, because JSONB document storage is a natural fit for aggregate persistence
- Good, because Marten includes its own event sourcing and projection support
- Good, because single library handles persistence, projections, and schema management
- Bad, because introduces a document DB abstraction over a relational database, adding conceptual complexity when relational modelling with EF Core + JSONB already satisfies our requirements
- Bad, because event sourcing is not a requirement for this project and Marten's added capabilities would be unused complexity
- Bad, because smaller community than EF Core; fewer team members will have prior experience

## More Information

- [EF Core documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/)
- [Dapper GitHub repository](https://github.com/DapperLib/Dapper)
- [CQRS with EF Core + Dapper — common .NET pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/cqrs-microservice-reads)

adrs.title: CQRS/Mediator — Custom Lightweight Mediator + Domain Events
adrs.verbatim:
## Context and Problem Statement

The application needs a clean architectural separation between operations that change state (commands) and operations that retrieve data (queries). This CQRS pattern reduces coupling between the write model and read model, and makes each handler independently testable. Alongside CQRS, a mediator is needed to dispatch commands and queries to their handlers without direct coupling between callers and handlers. Additionally, domain events are required to propagate side effects — particularly gamification triggers such as XP awards and achievement checks — without polluting command handlers with cross-cutting concerns. Which mediator library or approach should implement this pattern?

## Decision Drivers

- Licensing: must be usable commercially without per-deployment fees
- Simplicity: the mediator pattern itself is not complex; the solution should match that simplicity
- Dependency count: avoid pulling in a heavy framework for a thin abstraction
- Testability: handlers must be easily unit-testable in isolation
- Extensibility: support for pipeline behaviours (validation, logging, error handling) as cross-cutting concerns
- Domain event support: ability to publish notifications that fan out to multiple handlers

## Considered Options

- MediatR (commercial license as of v12+)
- Custom lightweight mediator
- Wolverine
- Immediate.Handlers

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Custom lightweight mediator", because the mediator pattern is trivially implementable in approximately 30–50 lines of C# using .NET's built-in dependency injection. MediatR became commercial in v12+, making it unsuitable for unrestricted use. The core interfaces — `IRequest<TResponse>`, `IRequestHandler<TRequest, TResponse>`, `INotification`, `INotificationHandler<T>` — and a dispatcher that resolves handlers from the DI container cover all requirements without external dependencies.

Domain events follow the `INotification` pattern and are published after `SaveChanges` to ensure consistency. The gamification chain — `TodoCompleted` -> `XpAwarded` -> `AchievementChecked` — is implemented as a sequence of notification handlers. Pipeline behaviours are registered as decorators in DI to handle validation, logging, and error normalisation as cross-cutting concerns.

### Positive Consequences

- Zero licensing cost or risk — we own the implementation entirely
- Interfaces are identical in shape to MediatR v11 (pre-commercial), making future migration trivial if needed
- Each command and query handler is a plain class with a single dependency — straightforward to unit test without mocking a mediator framework
- Pipeline behaviours are explicit decorator registrations in DI, visible and debuggable without framework magic
- Domain event fan-out via `INotification` cleanly decouples gamification side effects from core command logic
- No transitive NuGet dependencies introduced

### Negative Consequences

- The implementation must be written and owned by the team; bugs are ours to fix
- Community resources (blog posts, Stack Overflow answers) will reference MediatR rather than our custom implementation
- Advanced MediatR features (streams via `IStreamRequest`, `RequestPreProcessor` / `RequestPostProcessor` chains) are not available out of the box and must be implemented if required

### Neutral

- The ~30–50 line implementation lives in a `Mediator/` folder in the application layer and is immediately readable by any developer familiar with the pattern
- If requirements grow significantly (distributed messaging, sagas, outbox), Wolverine remains a viable upgrade path without requiring a full architecture change

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### MediatR (commercial license as of v12+)

The de facto .NET mediator library, widely adopted and well-documented. From v12 onward, commercial use requires a paid license.

- Good, because extensive community documentation and examples
- Good, because full-featured: pipeline behaviours, streaming requests, pre/post processors
- Good, because familiar to most .NET developers
- Bad, because v12+ requires a commercial license for production use — unacceptable ongoing cost for a thin abstraction we can own ourselves
- Bad, because locking in a commercial dependency for ~50 lines of infrastructure code is disproportionate

### Custom lightweight mediator

A hand-written implementation of the mediator pattern using interfaces resolved from .NET's built-in DI container.

- Good, because zero licensing cost or risk
- Good, because the team owns the code — no upstream breaking changes
- Good, because the implementation is small enough for any team member to read and understand in minutes
- Good, because interface shape can mirror MediatR v11 for community familiarity
- Bad, because the team is responsible for any bugs or gaps in the implementation
- Bad, because advanced features must be built when needed rather than pulled from a library

### Wolverine

A full-featured .NET messaging and command-handling framework with built-in support for outbox patterns, sagas, and distributed messaging.

- Good, because comprehensive feature set covering messaging, scheduling, and saga coordination
- Good, because built-in outbox support ensures reliable message delivery
- Good, because open-source and actively maintained
- Bad, because significantly more than needed for an in-process mediator — brings distributed messaging infrastructure into scope
- Bad, because heavier framework increases onboarding complexity and startup configuration
- Bad, because coupling application architecture to Wolverine's conventions is a larger commitment than a simple mediator

### Immediate.Handlers

A source-generator-based mediator for .NET that generates handler dispatch code at compile time.

- Good, because compile-time dispatch eliminates reflection overhead at runtime
- Good, because open-source with no licensing restrictions
- Bad, because smaller community and less battle-tested than MediatR or Wolverine
- Bad, because source generator tooling can complicate debugging and IDE integration
- Bad, because the compile-time generation model is less flexible for dynamic pipeline behaviour composition

## More Information

- [CQRS pattern overview — Microsoft Architecture Guides](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cqrs)
- [MediatR licensing change announcement (v12)](https://github.com/jbogard/MediatR/discussions/969)
- [Wolverine documentation](https://wolverinefx.net/)
- [Immediate.Handlers GitHub](https://github.com/ImmediateActions/Immediate.Handlers)
