- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-018-error-handling" status="accepted" title="Error Handling — Result Pattern + Problem Details (RFC 9457)" customLabel="ADR-018" /> — Error handling implemented as a pipeline behaviour
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-004-api-style" status="accepted" title="API Style — REST Minimal APIs + SignalR + Scalar API Docs" customLabel="ADR-004" /> — SignalR real-time updates triggered via domain events published through this mediator

adrs.title: CI/CD — GitHub Actions
adrs.verbatim:
## Context and Problem Statement

The EM2Devs.Todo project needs an automated pipeline that builds, tests, lints, scans, and deploys every change. Without automation, quality gates are manual and inconsistent, and the feedback loop for contributors is slow. The team needs a CI/CD platform that integrates tightly with the code host, supports .NET 9 workloads, and operates within a reasonable cost envelope. Which CI/CD platform should drive the pipeline?

## Decision Drivers

- GitHub integration: the repository is hosted on GitHub; the platform should reduce context-switching and integration friction
- .NET support: native or well-maintained action ecosystem for `dotnet build`, `dotnet test`, `dotnet format`, EF Core migrations
- Cost: free tier availability for a project at this scale; predictable pricing as usage grows
- Container registry support: the pipeline must be able to build and push Docker images without requiring a separate registry platform
- Community ecosystem: reusable actions for common steps (setup-dotnet, caching, Playwright, security scanning)
- Security scanning: the pipeline must include steps for dependency vulnerability checks and SAST

## Considered Options

- GitHub Actions
- Azure DevOps Pipelines
- GitLab CI

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "GitHub Actions", because the code is already hosted on GitHub, making Actions the path of least resistance — no separate account, no webhook configuration, no separate secrets store. The `actions/setup-dotnet` action has first-class .NET 9 support, caching is built in via `actions/cache`, and GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) is directly available for Docker image publishing. The ecosystem of community-maintained actions covers every step in the required pipeline without custom scripting.

The pipeline is structured into the following jobs, which run in dependency order:

| Job | Steps |
|-----|-------|
| `build` | Checkout, setup .NET 9, restore NuGet packages, `dotnet build --no-restore` |
| `lint` | `dotnet format --verify-no-changes`, ESLint, Prettier, svelte-check (ref: <AdrLink slug="20260305-016-code-quality" status="accepted" title="Code Quality — Analyzers, Formatters, Hooks, Conventional Commits/Branches" customLabel="ADR-016" />) |
| `test` | Unit tests (xUnit), integration tests via Testcontainers (ref: <AdrLink slug="20260305-014-testing" status="accepted" title="Testing — xUnit + Shouldly + NSubstitute + Testcontainers / Vitest + Playwright" customLabel="ADR-014" />) |
| `security` | `dotnet list package --vulnerable`, OWASP dependency-check, SAST scan (ref: [ADR-021]) |
| `migrate` | `dotnet ef database update` against a staging DB (ref: [ADR-020]) |
| `deploy` | Build Docker image, push to GHCR, deploy to target environment |

Branch protection rules require `build`, `lint`, `test`, and `security` to pass before any PR can merge.

### Positive Consequences

- Contributors get automated feedback (build status, test results, lint errors) directly in the PR without leaving GitHub
- GHCR eliminates the need for a separate container registry account; images are co-located with the code
- Reusable workflows and composite actions allow pipeline logic to be shared and versioned within the repo
- GitHub-native secrets management keeps credentials out of code with no additional tooling
- Free for public repositories; Actions minutes for private repos scale predictably

### Negative Consequences

- GitHub vendor lock-in: the pipeline syntax (YAML with GitHub-specific expressions) is not portable to other CI platforms without rewrite
- Actions minute limits apply on private repositories; compute-intensive integration tests must be managed to avoid unexpected billing
- GitHub Actions runners use Ubuntu by default; Windows-specific build steps require self-hosted runners or a paid runner tier

### Neutral

- The pipeline configuration lives in `.github/workflows/` within the monorepo (ref: <AdrLink slug="20260305-015-repo-structure" status="accepted" title="Repo Structure — Monorepo with Clean Architecture Layers" customLabel="ADR-015" />), versioned alongside the code it tests
- PR title validation (conventional commit format for squash-merge) is enforced as a separate workflow job

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### GitHub Actions

The native CI/CD platform for GitHub-hosted repositories, configured via YAML files in `.github/workflows/`.

- Good, because zero additional account setup — triggers, secrets, and environments are all configured in the same GitHub UI used for code review
- Good, because `actions/setup-dotnet` provides .NET 9 support and caching out of the box
- Good, because GHCR provides a free, integrated container registry with the same access control model as the repository
- Good, because free tier is generous for public repositories; community actions cover every required pipeline step
- Bad, because pipeline YAML uses GitHub-specific expression syntax, creating vendor lock-in
- Bad, because compute is limited for private repositories and can incur costs at scale

### Azure DevOps Pipelines

Microsoft's enterprise CI/CD platform, tightly integrated with the Azure ecosystem.

- Good, because first-class .NET support and a mature YAML pipeline syntax
- Good, because strong integration with Azure Container Registry, Azure App Service, and Azure Key Vault
- Bad, because the code lives on GitHub, requiring webhook configuration and cross-platform integration overhead
- Bad, because a separate Azure DevOps organisation must be created, maintained, and billed independently from GitHub
- Bad, because context-switching between GitHub (code review) and Azure DevOps (pipeline results) slows contributor feedback loops

### GitLab CI

A fully integrated DevOps platform with its own Git hosting, CI/CD, container registry, and security scanning.

- Good, because fully integrated platform covers code hosting, CI/CD, registry, and security scanning in one product
- Good, because pipeline syntax (`.gitlab-ci.yml`) is mature and well-documented
- Bad, because the project is hosted on GitHub; adopting GitLab CI would require migrating the repository to GitLab, which is a significant operational change with no corresponding benefit
- Bad, because contributors and stakeholders are already using GitHub workflows (issues, PRs, discussions); fragmenting the toolchain is not justified

## More Information

- [GitHub Actions documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/actions)
- [actions/setup-dotnet](https://github.com/actions/setup-dotnet)
- [GitHub Container Registry](https://docs.github.com/en/packages/working-with-a-github-packages-registry/working-with-the-container-registry)
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-014-testing" status="accepted" title="Testing — xUnit + Shouldly + NSubstitute + Testcontainers / Vitest + Playwright" customLabel="ADR-014" /> — Testing strategy; test jobs run in this pipeline
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-015-repo-structure" status="accepted" title="Repo Structure — Monorepo with Clean Architecture Layers" customLabel="ADR-015" /> — Repo structure; `.github/workflows/` is defined within the monorepo layout
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-016-code-quality" status="accepted" title="Code Quality — Analyzers, Formatters, Hooks, Conventional Commits/Branches" customLabel="ADR-016" /> — Code quality tools; linting and format verification run as pipeline jobs

adrs.title: Observability — Grafana Stack + Serilog + Aspire Dashboard
adrs.verbatim:
## Context and Problem Statement

A production-grade application requires visibility into all three observability signals: structured logs, runtime metrics, and distributed traces. Without this visibility, diagnosing failures, tracking performance regressions, and understanding system behaviour under load is guesswork. The gamification engine in particular — XP awards, streak tracking, achievement checks — produces background workloads whose execution must be traceable end-to-end. Additionally, the development inner loop should not require a full production observability stack to inspect traces and logs locally. Which observability tools and approach should cover both development and production?

## Decision Drivers

- Three signals coverage: logs, metrics, and traces must all be captured and queryable
- OpenTelemetry compatibility: signals should flow through the OTel standard to avoid vendor lock-in
- Aspire integration: the project already uses .NET Aspire, which configures OTel ServiceDefaults; the observability stack should build on that foundation rather than replace it
- Open-source: the production stack must be deployable without per-seat or per-host licensing fees
- .NET ecosystem fit: the structured logging library should be widely adopted in the .NET community and support rich property enrichment
- Development experience: developers should be able to inspect traces, logs, and metrics during local development without external accounts or heavy infrastructure setup

## Considered Options

- Grafana stack (Prometheus + Loki + Tempo + Grafana)
- Azure Monitor / Application Insights
- Datadog / New Relic
- Seq + Prometheus

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Multi-layer approach using Aspire Dashboard for development and Grafana stack for production, with Serilog as the structured logging library throughout", because it covers all three observability signals with open-source tools, integrates cleanly with the OTel pipeline that Aspire ServiceDefaults already configures, and provides a zero-config inner loop experience for developers.

The approach has three layers:

**Development (local):** The .NET Aspire Dashboard (`aspire-dashboard`) provides built-in trace, log, and metric visualisation at zero configuration cost. It is automatically available when running via the AppHost. Developers can inspect traces for any request or background job without setting up Prometheus or Grafana locally.

**Production:** The Grafana stack runs in containers:
- **Prometheus** — scrapes metrics exposed by the `aspire-dashboard` OTel metrics endpoint and application `/metrics` endpoint
- **Loki** — receives structured log streams forwarded from the OTel log exporter
- **Tempo** — receives distributed traces via the OTel OTLP exporter
- **Grafana** — unified dashboard layer querying Prometheus, Loki, and Tempo; supports correlation between signals (e.g., click a log line to jump to its trace)

**Structured logging:** Serilog is used throughout the .NET backend. It is the de facto standard for structured logging in the .NET community, with a rich enricher ecosystem (request IDs, correlation IDs, machine name, environment). The OTel sink (`Serilog.Sinks.OpenTelemetry`) routes log events into the same OTel pipeline already configured by Aspire ServiceDefaults, meaning logs, metrics, and traces share the same propagation context.

During development, the Grafana stack containers can optionally be started via Aspire AppHost resource definitions, mirroring the production topology for debugging production-specific observability behaviour.

### Positive Consequences

- All three signals are correlated through shared OTel trace and span IDs, enabling root-cause analysis that jumps between logs, metrics, and traces for the same request
- Aspire Dashboard provides immediate, zero-cost observability during the development inner loop; developers can inspect gamification event chains (TodoCompleted -> XpAwarded -> AchievementChecked) as traces without any infrastructure overhead
- Grafana's unified query layer (Explore) lets operators navigate from a Prometheus metric spike to the contributing Loki log lines to the Tempo trace, all in one tool
- The OTel-first design means the backend emits to an OTel collector; swapping the backend storage (e.g., replacing Tempo with Jaeger) requires only exporter reconfiguration, not code changes
- Serilog's enricher pipeline ensures every log event carries correlation IDs and request context automatically

### Negative Consequences

- Self-hosting Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, and Grafana in production requires operational capacity: upgrades, storage sizing for Loki and Tempo, Prometheus retention management
- Grafana stack container configuration (datasource provisioning, dashboard JSON) must be version-controlled and maintained alongside the application
- The OTel sink for Serilog (`Serilog.Sinks.OpenTelemetry`) adds a NuGet dependency; if the sink lags behind the OTel SDK version, compatibility issues may arise

### Neutral

- Grafana Alloy (formerly Agent) can be introduced later as an OTel Collector replacement if centralised scraping, buffering, or transformation of signals is needed in production
- Aspire Dashboard is development-only; it does not provide long-term signal retention and is not a production replacement for the Grafana stack

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Grafana Stack (Prometheus + Loki + Tempo + Grafana)

A composable, open-source observability stack where each component handles one signal and Grafana provides unified querying and dashboarding.

- Good, because fully open-source with no per-host or per-seat licensing
- Good, because each component integrates natively with OTel exporters; no proprietary SDK required
- Good, because Grafana's correlation features (Explore, exemplars, trace-to-logs links) connect all three signals in a single UI
- Good, because containerised deployment via Docker Compose or Aspire resource definitions mirrors the production topology during development
- Bad, because self-hosting adds operational overhead: storage, retention policies, and upgrades must be managed
- Bad, because initial setup (datasource provisioning, dashboards) requires upfront configuration work

### Azure Monitor / Application Insights

Microsoft's managed observability service, tightly integrated with Azure hosting.

- Good, because fully managed; no infrastructure to operate
- Good, because first-class .NET SDK integration and automatic instrumentation for ASP.NET Core
- Bad, because Azure-specific; creates lock-in that limits portability to other cloud providers
- Bad, because costs at scale (data ingestion, retention) can grow significantly; pricing is per GB ingested
- Bad, because the Application Insights SDK is a proprietary layer on top of OTel, making future migration harder

### Datadog / New Relic

Commercial SaaS observability platforms with comprehensive out-of-the-box integrations.

- Good, because turn-key setup with auto-instrumentation, dashboards, and alerting included
- Good, because no infrastructure to operate; managed retention and scaling
- Bad, because high per-host or per-user SaaS costs are disproportionate for a project at this scale
- Bad, because proprietary agents and SDKs introduce vendor lock-in at the instrumentation level

### Seq + Prometheus

Seq provides excellent structured log search and dashboarding for .NET applications; Prometheus handles metrics separately.

- Good, because Seq is purpose-built for .NET structured logs and has a polished search UI
- Good, because Prometheus is the de facto standard for metrics
- Bad, because Seq does not handle distributed traces; a third tool (e.g., Jaeger) would still be needed for full three-signal coverage
- Bad, because Seq has a commercial license for teams; Loki is a like-for-like open-source alternative that integrates directly with Grafana
- Bad, because two separate UIs (Seq for logs, Grafana for metrics/traces) reduce the ability to correlate signals in one place

## More Information

- [OpenTelemetry .NET SDK](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/net/)
- [Serilog OpenTelemetry sink](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-sinks-opentelemetry)
- [Grafana Loki documentation](https://grafana.com/docs/loki/latest/)
- [Grafana Tempo documentation](https://grafana.com/docs/tempo/latest/)
- [Aspire Dashboard documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/aspire/fundamentals/dashboard/overview)

adrs.title: Frontend State Management — Svelte 5 Runes + Stores + SvelteKit Load Functions
adrs.verbatim:
## Context and Problem Statement

EM2Devs.Todo is a gamified todo application with three distinct categories of state: component-local UI state (form inputs, modal visibility, animation triggers), cross-cutting shared state that multiple unrelated components must read and write (authenticated user identity, XP/level display, notification queue), and server-loaded page data (todo lists, quest details, leaderboard rankings). The chosen SvelteKit / Svelte 5 framework (<AdrLink slug="20260305-002-frontend-framework" status="accepted" title="Frontend Framework — SvelteKit / Svelte 5" customLabel="ADR-002" />) ships multiple built-in mechanisms for handling each category. The question is whether those built-in tools are sufficient, or whether an external state management library should be added. What state management strategy should the EM2Devs.Todo SvelteKit frontend follow?

## Decision Drivers

- Svelte 5 ecosystem alignment: prefer patterns the Svelte 5 compiler and SvelteKit runtime are designed to support natively
- Simplicity: avoid external dependencies that add cognitive overhead, bundle weight, or fight against Svelte's reactive model
- Reactivity performance: gamification state (XP counters, streak timers, achievement progress) changes frequently and must propagate efficiently
- SSR compatibility: server-side rendering must work without client-only state assumptions
- Developer experience: patterns should be discoverable, composable, and easy to reason about for a small team
- Minimal boilerplate: the overhead of any pattern must be proportional to the complexity it manages

## Considered Options

- Svelte 5 built-in tools (runes + stores + SvelteKit load functions + context API)
- External state management library (Zustand/Jotai-style adapter for Svelte)
- Redux-style global store (svelte-redux or hand-rolled flux pattern)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Svelte 5 built-in tools", because the four built-in mechanisms together cover every state category this application has without requiring an external dependency. Each mechanism is scoped to the exact problem it solves, which keeps patterns predictable and avoids the "put everything in the global store" anti-pattern that external libraries tend to encourage.

The four mechanisms and their designated roles are:

- **Runes (`$state`, `$derived`, `$effect`)** — component-local state and derived values. This is the primary reactive primitive for anything scoped to a single component or a small composable function. Replaces Svelte 4's `let` + `$:` reactive declarations with an explicit, compiler-checked API.
- **SvelteKit `load` functions** — server-side and universal data loading for route and layout data. Handles SSR, streaming, cache invalidation (`invalidate()`), and dependent data waterfalls. Used for fetching todos, quests, leaderboard data, and user profiles. Data returned from `load` is available as the `data` prop on the corresponding page component.
- **Svelte stores (`writable`, `readable`, `derived`)** — cross-cutting shared state that unrelated components need to access. Used for auth state (current user session), the notification/toast queue, and the XP/level values rendered in the global header. Stores are compatible with SSR when initialised correctly.
- **Context API (`setContext` / `getContext`)** — scoped dependency injection within a component subtree. Used to pass a "current quest" or "active collection" object down a deep component tree without threading props through every intermediate component.

This layered approach means no single mechanism becomes a dumping ground for all state. Engineers follow a clear decision rule: is this state local to one component? Use runes. Is it page or layout data loaded from the server? Use a `load` function. Do multiple unrelated components across the tree need it? Use a store. Does a parent need to share something with deep children in a bounded subtree? Use context.

### Positive Consequences

- Zero additional dependencies — the state management layer has no npm packages to update, audit, or keep compatible with SvelteKit upgrades
- Each pattern matches the Svelte 5 compiler's expectations; runes, stores, and load functions all integrate with Svelte's devtools and HMR without special adapters
- SSR is safe by design: `load` functions run on the server, stores can be seeded from server data, and runes are component-scoped and therefore not shared across requests
- The decision rule (local / server-loaded / cross-cutting / scoped tree) is teachable and eliminates bikeshedding about where to put new state
- Bundle size is not increased by any external library

### Negative Consequences

- There is no single place to inspect all application state; developers accustomed to Redux DevTools will find per-component rune state and distributed stores harder to trace across the whole app
- Svelte 5 runes are a significant shift from Svelte 4 patterns; developers with Svelte 4 experience must unlearn `$:` reactive declarations and `export let` for shared state
- Large-scale data normalisation (e.g., caching and deduplicating nested todo/quest relationships) is not handled out of the box — if the data model grows complex, a query-cache library (like TanStack Query for Svelte) may be needed as a targeted addition

### Neutral

- Svelte stores use the subscriber pattern and are not tied to Svelte's component lifecycle, making them usable in plain TypeScript modules (e.g., service classes) as well as components
- The context API is not global — it does not leak across unrelated component trees, which is intentional but means it cannot replace stores for app-wide state

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Svelte 5 built-in tools (runes + stores + load functions + context API)

Four complementary mechanisms shipped with Svelte 5 and SvelteKit, each optimised for a different state scope.

- Good, because no external dependency is needed — the installed framework already provides all required primitives
- Good, because runes are fine-grained and compile-time checked; `$derived` values are memoised automatically without manual dependency arrays
- Good, because SvelteKit `load` functions handle SSR, streaming, and cache invalidation as first-class concerns — server state does not need a separate client-side caching layer for this app's scale
- Good, because Svelte stores are reactive to the auto-subscription shorthand (`$storeName`) in templates, making cross-component state feel as natural as local state
- Good, because the context API prevents prop drilling in deep trees without polluting a global namespace
- Bad, because there is no unified devtools view of all state — debugging requires checking component state, stores, and load data separately
- Bad, because the decision rule requires discipline; without code review enforcement, engineers may reach for stores when runes suffice, or bypass `load` functions in favour of client-side fetching

### External state management library (Zustand/Jotai-style adapter for Svelte)

Libraries like `svelte-zustand` or custom atom-based stores that mirror patterns popular in the React ecosystem.

- Good, because developers with React/Zustand experience can transfer mental models directly
- Good, because atom-based libraries provide fine-grained subscriptions that avoid over-rendering
- Bad, because Svelte stores already provide a subscribable primitive — an external atom library largely duplicates it with extra indirection
- Bad, because any external library must be maintained for Svelte 5 compatibility; the Svelte 5 runes model is new and many React-ecosystem adapters have not caught up
- Bad, because adds a dependency and onboarding overhead for a problem the built-in tools already solve at this app's scale

### Redux-style global store (svelte-redux or hand-rolled flux)

A single global state tree with explicit actions and reducers, following the Flux/Redux pattern.

- Good, because all state transitions are explicit and traceable through a reducer function — good for complex workflows with many actors
- Good, because Redux DevTools can be wired in to provide a time-travel debugging experience
- Bad, because this is significant over-engineering for a single-frontend app; the todos/quests/XP domain does not have the multi-actor, multi-system state synchronisation problems that Redux was designed to solve
- Bad, because the ceremony of defining action types, action creators, and reducers for every state change is disproportionate to the complexity of the state being managed
- Bad, because Redux's synchronous reducer model does not integrate naturally with SvelteKit `load` functions, creating a seam where server-loaded data must be manually pushed into the store on page navigation

## More Information

- [Svelte 5 Runes — $state, $derived, $effect](https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/what-are-runes)
- [Svelte stores (writable, readable, derived)](https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/stores)
- [SvelteKit load functions](https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/load)
- [Svelte context API (setContext / getContext)](https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/context)

## Context and Problem Statement

EM2Devs.Todo spans a .NET 9 backend (API, application layer, domain, infrastructure) and a SvelteKit frontend. Both require a test strategy that enables confident refactoring, prevents regressions, and exercises integration points (database, cache, auth) with real dependencies where it matters. The testing stack must be open-source licensed for unrestricted commercial use, readable, and well-suited to the Clean Architecture layer structure. A notable constraint is that FluentAssertions — formerly the de facto .NET assertion library — moved to a commercial license in v7+, requiring an alternative assertion library for backend tests.

## Decision Drivers

- Open-source licensing: all test libraries must be usable without commercial licenses or per-deployment fees
- Assertion readability: assertion failures should produce clear, human-readable messages that identify what was expected vs. what was found
- .NET ecosystem maturity: libraries must be actively maintained with broad community adoption
- Container-based integration tests: infrastructure integration tests should exercise a real PostgreSQL instance and Redis cache, not in-memory fakes, to catch driver-level and query-level issues
- Architecture boundary enforcement: the Clean Architecture layer structure must be machine-verifiable to prevent dependency drift
- Frontend testing DX: frontend tooling must integrate with Vite/SvelteKit's build pipeline natively
- E2E coverage: critical user flows must be tested against the real application in a browser

## Considered Options

- Assertion library: Shouldly, FluentAssertions (v7+), TUnit, xUnit built-in Assert
- Mocking library: NSubstitute, Moq
- Integration testing: WebApplicationFactory + Testcontainers, in-memory EF Core provider
- Frontend unit/component: Vitest + Svelte Testing Library, Jest + @testing-library/svelte
- E2E: Playwright, Cypress

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "xUnit + Shouldly + NSubstitute + Testcontainers for backend; Vitest + Svelte Testing Library + Playwright for frontend", because this combination covers all test levels with open-source tools, provides readable assertion output, and exercises real infrastructure in integration tests.

**Backend test stack:**

| Tool | Role |
|------|------|
| xUnit | Test runner and framework — industry standard for .NET; first-class support in `dotnet test` and CI |
| Shouldly | Assertion library — open-source, readable `Should()` extension syntax, clear failure messages |
| NSubstitute | Mocking — clean substitute creation syntax; avoids Moq's setup verbosity |
| WebApplicationFactory | ASP.NET Core in-process test host for integration tests |
| Testcontainers | Spins up real PostgreSQL and Redis containers per test session; no in-memory fakes for integration layer |
| NetArchTest | Architecture tests — enforces that Domain has no Infrastructure references, Application has no API references, etc. |

**Frontend test stack:**

| Tool | Role |
|------|------|
| Vitest | Unit/component test runner — Vite-native, shares config with SvelteKit build, fast HMR-aware test execution |
| Svelte Testing Library | Component testing utilities for Svelte — encourages testing behaviour, not implementation |
| Playwright | E2E browser tests — cross-browser, Microsoft-backed, first-class TypeScript support |

**Test project naming convention** (per Clean Architecture layer, ref: <AdrLink slug="20260305-015-repo-structure" status="accepted" title="Repo Structure — Monorepo with Clean Architecture Layers" customLabel="ADR-015" />):

```
tests/
├── EM2Devs.Todo.Api.UnitTests/
├── EM2Devs.Todo.Application.UnitTests/
├── EM2Devs.Todo.Domain.UnitTests/
├── EM2Devs.Todo.Infrastructure.IntegrationTests/
└── EM2Devs.Todo.E2E/                              # Playwright
```

Architecture tests live in a dedicated project (`EM2Devs.Todo.ArchitectureTests`) that references all production assemblies but contains no application logic.

### Positive Consequences

- Shouldly provides assertion output that reads as natural English (`value.ShouldBe(42)`) and failure messages that immediately identify the discrepancy without requiring a debugger
- Testcontainers ensures integration tests exercise the real PostgreSQL wire protocol, real EF Core migrations, and real Redis client behaviour — bugs invisible with in-memory providers are caught before deployment
- NetArchTest assertions are executable specifications of the Clean Architecture rules; violations fail the CI build rather than requiring manual code review
- Vitest shares the Vite config with SvelteKit, eliminating the configuration drift between the test environment and the build environment
- Playwright's `codegen` tool accelerates E2E test authoring; its trace viewer provides step-by-step replay of failures in CI

### Negative Consequences

- Testcontainers requires Docker to be available on the CI runner; GitHub Actions' default Ubuntu runners satisfy this, but developers on machines without Docker Desktop must install an alternative runtime (e.g., Colima on macOS)
- Shouldly is less widely documented than FluentAssertions; developers familiar with FluentAssertions will need a brief ramp-up period, though the API is similar in structure
- Maintaining separate test runners (xUnit for .NET, Vitest for frontend, Playwright for E2E) means the CI pipeline must configure and cache three distinct toolchains

### Neutral

- xUnit's `[Theory]` + `[InlineData]` / `[MemberData]` provides parameterised test support equivalent to NUnit's `[TestCase]`, covering all common data-driven test scenarios
- Aspire's test project support (Microsoft.Extensions.AspNetCore.Testing) is available for integration tests that need the full Aspire orchestration; this is considered for future adoption as needed

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Shouldly

A mature open-source assertion library for .NET. Assertion failures include the asserted expression, expected value, and actual value in a human-readable format.

- Good, because open-source with no commercial licensing restrictions
- Good, because `Should()` extension method syntax reads naturally: `result.ShouldBe(expected)`, `collection.ShouldContain(item)`
- Good, because failure messages include the source expression, reducing time spent reading stack traces
- Good, because actively maintained with .NET 9 support
- Bad, because smaller community than FluentAssertions; fewer blog posts and Stack Overflow answers reference it directly

### FluentAssertions (v7+)

The formerly dominant .NET assertion library, now requiring a commercial license for production use from v7 onward.

- Good, because extensive community documentation and the widest existing example base
- Good, because highly expressive chained assertions covering objects, collections, exceptions, and async code
- Bad, because v7+ requires a commercial license — unacceptable for a project committed to open-source tooling
- Bad, because adopting it creates a recurring license obligation for a component that can be replaced by open-source alternatives without meaningful loss of capability

### TUnit

A newer .NET test framework built on source generators and the Microsoft.Testing.Platform.

- Good, because source-generator-based discovery is faster than reflection-based runners at scale
- Good, because open-source and designed for modern .NET
- Bad, because newer and less battle-tested than xUnit; community resources, CI integrations, and IDE support are maturing
- Bad, because switching from xUnit would require rewriting existing test patterns; the benefit does not outweigh the migration cost at this stage

### xUnit built-in Assert

The assertion methods included in xUnit itself (`Assert.Equal`, `Assert.Contains`, etc.).

- Good, because zero additional dependency
- Good, because always version-compatible with xUnit
- Bad, because assertion messages are less informative than Shouldly's — failure output requires manual inspection to understand the discrepancy
- Bad, because the static `Assert.X(expected, actual)` syntax is less readable than fluent extension methods

### NSubstitute vs. Moq

NSubstitute uses a natural substitution syntax (`Substitute.For<IService>()`, `sub.Method(arg).Returns(value)`) that mirrors how you would describe the interaction in English. Moq requires `Mock<T>` wrappers and `.Object` dereferencing for the substitute instance.

- NSubstitute good, because cleaner setup syntax reduces test boilerplate
- NSubstitute good, because verification syntax (`sub.Received().Method(arg)`) reads more naturally than Moq's `mock.Verify(m => m.Method(arg), Times.Once())`
- Moq bad, because the `mock.Object` indirection adds noise in test setup; NSubstitute instances are used directly

### WebApplicationFactory + Testcontainers vs. in-memory EF Core provider

- Testcontainers good, because real PostgreSQL catches query syntax issues, transaction behaviour, and migration correctness that in-memory providers silently ignore
- Testcontainers good, because test environment mirrors production database engine, eliminating a class of "works in tests, fails in prod" bugs
- In-memory EF Core bad, because it does not enforce relational constraints, does not execute raw SQL, and does not run migrations — it is a fake, not a real integration surface

### Vitest vs. Jest

- Vitest good, because it shares the Vite config with SvelteKit, avoiding a separate Jest + Babel + SvelteKit transform pipeline that frequently diverges from the production build
- Vitest good, because HMR-aware test execution provides a fast feedback loop during development
- Jest bad, because requires separate transform configuration to understand Svelte components; configuration drift from the Vite build pipeline is a recurring maintenance burden

### Playwright vs. Cypress

- Playwright good, because Microsoft-backed with active .NET and TypeScript investment; long-term support trajectory is strong
- Playwright good, because cross-browser testing (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit) in a single tool
- Playwright good, because trace viewer provides a recorded, step-by-step replay of test failures, making CI failure diagnosis dramatically faster
- Cypress bad, because historically limited to Chromium-based browsers for E2E; multi-browser support was added later and remains secondary
- Cypress bad, because Cypress Cloud (for CI parallelisation and test recording) is a paid service; Playwright's tracing is built-in

## More Information

- [Shouldly documentation](https://docs.shouldly.org/)
- [NSubstitute documentation](https://nsubstitute.github.io/)
- [Testcontainers for .NET](https://dotnet.testcontainers.org/)
- [NetArchTest](https://github.com/BenMorris/NetArchTest)
- [Vitest documentation](https://vitest.dev/)
- [Playwright documentation](https://playwright.dev/)
- [FluentAssertions commercial license announcement](https://fluentassertions.com/about/)
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-011-ci-cd" status="accepted" title="CI/CD — GitHub Actions" customLabel="ADR-011" /> — All test jobs run in the GitHub Actions pipeline
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-015-repo-structure" status="accepted" title="Repo Structure — Monorepo with Clean Architecture Layers" customLabel="ADR-015" /> — Test project layout follows the naming conventions defined there

## Context and Problem Statement

The EM2Devs.Todo project consists of multiple distinct concerns: a .NET 9 Minimal API backend, a SvelteKit frontend, an Aspire AppHost orchestrator, shared Aspire ServiceDefaults, EF Core migrations, and multiple test projects. These components must be co-located in a way that makes the Clean Architecture layer boundaries explicit, keeps project naming consistent and predictable, enables Aspire's project reference model to function correctly, and allows a developer new to the codebase to orient themselves quickly. How should the repository be structured?

## Decision Drivers

- Clean Architecture compliance: the directory layout must reinforce the Domain → Application → Infrastructure → Api dependency direction; layer boundaries should be visible at a glance
- Aspire project structure: the AppHost must reference all service projects; placing everything in a single `src/` tree makes relative project references straightforward
- Naming convention: all .NET projects follow the `EM2Devs.Todo.{Concern}` convention to communicate project purpose without ambiguity and to keep NuGet package IDs consistent if packages are ever published
- Test organisation: test projects are separated from production source to prevent accidental production references to test-only packages; tests are organised per Clean Architecture concern
- Developer navigation: a developer unfamiliar with the codebase should be able to infer where a feature's logic lives by reading the directory tree alone

## Considered Options

- Monorepo with Clean Architecture layer structure (all projects under `src/`, all tests under `tests/`)
- Monorepo with feature-first organisation (features as top-level directories containing their own API, domain, and test subdirectories)
- Polyrepo (separate repositories for frontend and backend)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Monorepo with Clean Architecture layers", because it keeps the entire delivery unit — backend, frontend, orchestration, and tests — under a single version history, simplifies cross-cutting changes (e.g., updating a shared NuGet version affects all projects in one PR), and makes the Clean Architecture dependency direction explicit at the file-system level.

**Repository layout:**

```
em2devs-apps-todo/
├── docs/
│   └── decisions/                                 # ADRs (managed by log4brains)
├── src/
│   ├── EM2Devs.Todo.AppHost/                      # .NET Aspire orchestrator — references all service projects
│   ├── EM2Devs.Todo.ServiceDefaults/              # Shared Aspire config: OTel, health checks, resilience
│   ├── EM2Devs.Todo.Api/                          # .NET 9 Minimal API — endpoint definitions, filters, middleware
│   ├── EM2Devs.Todo.Domain/                       # Domain models, value objects, domain events, interfaces
│   ├── EM2Devs.Todo.Application/                  # CQRS commands, queries, handlers, validators (ref: ADR-010)
│   ├── EM2Devs.Todo.Infrastructure/               # EF Core DbContext, Dapper queries, Auth0, Redis (ref: ADR-009)
│   └── EM2Devs.Todo.Web/                          # SvelteKit frontend (ref: ADR-002)
├── tests/
│   ├── EM2Devs.Todo.Api.UnitTests/                # API endpoint and middleware unit tests
│   ├── EM2Devs.Todo.Application.UnitTests/        # Command/query handler unit tests
│   ├── EM2Devs.Todo.Domain.UnitTests/             # Domain model and domain event unit tests
│   ├── EM2Devs.Todo.Infrastructure.IntegrationTests/  # EF Core + PostgreSQL + Redis (Testcontainers)
│   ├── EM2Devs.Todo.ArchitectureTests/            # NetArchTest — enforces Clean Architecture boundaries
│   └── EM2Devs.Todo.E2E/                          # Playwright end-to-end tests (ref: ADR-014)
├── .github/
│   └── workflows/                                 # GitHub Actions pipeline definitions (ref: ADR-011)
├── .editorconfig                                   # Compiler-enforced formatting rules
├── Directory.Build.props                           # Centralised NuGet versions, shared analyzer config
├── EM2Devs.Todo.sln                               # Solution file referencing all src/ and tests/ projects
└── README.md
```

**Clean Architecture dependency rule** (enforced by `EM2Devs.Todo.ArchitectureTests`):

```
Domain  <──  Application  <──  Infrastructure
                    ^                ^
                    └──── Api ───────┘
```

Domain has no references to other application projects. Application references Domain only. Infrastructure references Domain and Application (for interfaces). Api references Application and Infrastructure (for DI registration).

**Naming convention:** All .NET projects follow `EM2Devs.Todo.{Concern}`, where `{Concern}` communicates the Clean Architecture layer (`Domain`, `Application`, `Infrastructure`, `Api`) or infrastructure role (`AppHost`, `ServiceDefaults`). Test projects append the test type: `.UnitTests`, `.IntegrationTests`, `.ArchitectureTests`, `.E2E`.

**`Directory.Build.props`** at the repository root centralises:
- `<TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>` for all .NET projects
- `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` and `<ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>`
- Shared NuGet package versions (central package management)
- Shared analyzer configuration (SonarAnalyzer, StyleCop)

### Positive Consequences

- A single `git clone` gives a developer everything needed to run the full stack via Aspire AppHost — no separate frontend or backend clone required
- Cross-cutting changes (e.g., bumping a shared NuGet version, renaming a domain type) are atomic: one PR, one review, one merge
- The Clean Architecture layer boundaries are visible as first-class directory names; a developer can navigate to the correct project by reading the folder name alone
- `Directory.Build.props` eliminates version drift between projects and reduces the maintenance surface for build configuration
- Architecture tests enforce the dependency rules at CI time, preventing accidental layer violations from accumulating silently

### Negative Consequences

- The solution file grows as the project grows; large solutions can be slower to load in IDEs without filtering
- Frontend (`EM2Devs.Todo.Web`) and backend live in the same repository; a team that wants to give the frontend team a minimal clone experience would need sparse checkout, which adds tooling complexity
- `Directory.Build.props` centralisation means a misconfiguration affects all projects simultaneously; care is required when modifying it

### Neutral

- The SvelteKit frontend is a Node.js project and does not participate in the `.sln` solution file; it is included in the monorepo as a directory within `src/` alongside the .NET projects
- Aspire's `EM2Devs.Todo.AppHost` project references the .NET service projects directly via `<ProjectReference>`; the SvelteKit frontend is launched by Aspire as an npm process resource

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Monorepo with Clean Architecture layers

All components live in one repository, organised by Clean Architecture concern under `src/` and by test type under `tests/`.

- Good, because atomic cross-cutting changes — one PR covers backend, frontend, and tests for a feature
- Good, because single `dotnet run --project src/EM2Devs.Todo.AppHost` starts the entire stack
- Good, because `Directory.Build.props` and `.editorconfig` apply consistently across all projects without duplication
- Good, because Clean Architecture layer names are first-class in the directory tree, making navigation intuitive
- Bad, because repository grows in size and scope as the project matures; eventually may warrant a split

### Monorepo with feature-first organisation

Top-level directories represent features (e.g., `todos/`, `achievements/`, `auth/`), each containing their own API routes, domain models, and tests.

- Good, because all code related to a feature is co-located — a developer working on achievements touches only one top-level directory
- Bad, because Clean Architecture boundaries are not visible in the directory structure; enforcing them requires stricter tooling and convention
- Bad, because shared infrastructure (EF Core DbContext, auth middleware) does not belong cleanly to any single feature and becomes an unnamed residual directory
- Bad, because Aspire project references and solution structure do not map cleanly to a feature-first layout

### Polyrepo (separate frontend and backend repositories)

Frontend and backend live in separate repositories, potentially with a third repository for shared types or contracts.

- Good, because independent deployment pipelines; frontend can deploy without triggering backend CI
- Good, because teams can be granted scoped access to only the relevant repository
- Bad, because cross-cutting changes (e.g., adding a new API endpoint that the frontend consumes) require coordinated PRs across multiple repositories
- Bad, because shared configuration (linting rules, commit conventions) must be duplicated or extracted to a separate config repository
- Bad, because at the project's current scale, the operational overhead of managing multiple repositories outweighs the isolation benefit

## More Information

- [Clean Architecture — Robert C. Martin](https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2012/08/13/the-clean-architecture.html)
- [.NET Aspire project structure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/aspire/fundamentals/app-host-overview)
- [MSBuild Directory.Build.props](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/msbuild/customize-by-directory)
- [NetArchTest](https://github.com/BenMorris/NetArchTest)
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-005-orchestration" status="accepted" title="Orchestration — .NET Aspire" customLabel="ADR-005" /> — Aspire AppHost references all service projects within this structure
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-014-testing" status="accepted" title="Testing — xUnit + Shouldly + NSubstitute + Testcontainers / Vitest + Playwright" customLabel="ADR-014" /> — Test project naming and organisation defined here
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-011-ci-cd" status="accepted" title="CI/CD — GitHub Actions" customLabel="ADR-011" /> — GitHub Actions workflows live in `.github/workflows/` within this layout
- Related: <AdrLink slug="20260305-016-code-quality" status="accepted" title="Code Quality — Analyzers, Formatters, Hooks, Conventional Commits/Branches" customLabel="ADR-016" /> — `.editorconfig` and `Directory.Build.props` are root-level files in this structure

## Context and Problem Statement

A codebase maintained by multiple contributors accumulates style inconsistencies, suppressible linting warnings, and ad-hoc commit messages unless quality gates are enforced automatically. Manual code review is insufficient for mechanical quality concerns — reviewers should focus on logic and architecture, not formatting or naming conventions. Additionally, conventional commit messages and branch names are prerequisites for automated changelog generation and predictable release management. Which code quality tools, enforcement points, and conventions should be adopted across the .NET backend and SvelteKit frontend?

## Decision Drivers

- Automated enforcement: quality rules must be enforced by tooling, not by convention or reviewer vigilance
- Pre-commit/pre-push validation: formatting and linting errors should be caught locally before a push, not only in CI
- CI enforcement: the pipeline must act as the final authority — what passes CI is what is acceptable
- Consistent style: the same style rules must apply whether a developer uses VS Code, Rider, or Visual Studio
- Conventional changelog support: commit messages must follow a machine-parseable format to enable automated changelog and release note generation
- Dual-stack coverage: both .NET (C#) and SvelteKit (TypeScript/Svelte) require their own idiomatic toolchains

## Considered Options

- Backend static analysis: SonarAnalyzer + StyleCop.Analyzers vs. Roslynator vs. analyzer-only approach
- Backend formatting: `dotnet format` (built-in) vs. CSharpier
- Frontend linting: ESLint + eslint-plugin-svelte vs. Biome
- Frontend formatting: Prettier + prettier-plugin-svelte vs. Biome
- Git hooks: Husky + lint-staged vs. lefthook vs. no hooks (CI-only enforcement)
- Commit convention: Conventional Commits vs. no enforced format

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Multi-layer enforcement — analyzers and formatters per stack, Husky + lint-staged for local hooks, Conventional Commits enforced via commitlint, and conventional branch naming enforced in both pre-push hook and CI", because it places quality checks at the earliest possible point (staged file check on commit), prevents bad commits from entering the remote (pre-push branch name check), and provides a CI safety net that is authoritative.

**Backend (.NET) quality layer:**

| Tool | Role |
|------|------|
| `.editorconfig` | Defines indentation, line endings, naming rules, and code style; enforced by the Roslyn compiler — violations are build warnings or errors, not just style suggestions |
| `dotnet format` | Auto-formatter; run on staged files by pre-commit hook; CI runs `dotnet format --verify-no-changes` to fail on any deviation |
| SonarAnalyzer.CSharp | Static analysis for bugs, code smells, security hotspots, and complexity — Roslyn-based, runs on every build |
| StyleCop.Analyzers | Additional style rules (XML documentation, member ordering, file layout); configured in `.editorconfig` |
| `Directory.Build.props` | Centralises NuGet versions for all analyzer packages; sets `<TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>` for release builds |

**Frontend (SvelteKit) quality layer:**

| Tool | Role |
|------|------|
| ESLint + eslint-plugin-svelte | Linting for TypeScript and Svelte components — catches unused variables, accessibility violations, Svelte-specific anti-patterns |
| Prettier + prettier-plugin-svelte | Opinionated formatting for `.ts`, `.svelte`, `.json`, `.css` files |
| svelte-check | Type-checking for `.svelte` files using the TypeScript compiler; run in CI to surface type errors in component props and bindings |

**Git hooks (Husky + lint-staged):**

Pre-commit hook runs lint-staged, which applies formatters and linters only to staged files — not the entire codebase. This keeps the hook fast even in a large monorepo.

```
Pre-commit (lint-staged):
  *.cs          →  dotnet format (format staged .cs files)
  *.ts, *.svelte →  prettier --write, eslint --fix
  *.json, *.css  →  prettier --write
```

Pre-push hook validates that the branch name matches the conventional branch pattern before the push reaches the remote:

```
Allowed branch patterns:
  feat/<short-description>
  fix/<short-description>
  chore/<short-description>
  hotfix/<short-description>
  release/<version>
  main
```

**Conventional Commits** are enforced via `commitlint` (`@commitlint/config-conventional`) in a commit-msg hook. The allowed types are: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`, `perf`, `ci`, `build`, `revert`. This enables automated changelog generation with `conventional-changelog` or `release-please`.

Example valid commit messages:
```
feat(achievements): add streak freeze power-up
fix(api): return 404 when todo not found instead of 500
chore(deps): bump SonarAnalyzer.CSharp to 9.32
```

**CI enforcement** (ref: <AdrLink slug="20260305-011-ci-cd" status="accepted" title="CI/CD — GitHub Actions" customLabel="ADR-011" />):
- `lint` job: `dotnet format --verify-no-changes`, `eslint`, `prettier --check`, `svelte-check`
- PR branch name validated against conventional branch pattern on PR creation event
- PR title validated against Conventional Commits format (used as squash-merge commit message)

### Positive Consequences

- Formatting debates are eliminated — `dotnet format` and Prettier produce deterministic output; there is no room for style bikeshedding in code review
- SonarAnalyzer catches a meaningful class of bugs (null dereference, resource leak, improper exception handling) at build time rather than in production
- Conventional commit messages enable automated changelog generation and release tagging via `release-please` or `conventional-changelog` without manual curation
- `lint-staged` applies hooks only to staged files, keeping the pre-commit hook under one second for typical change sizes
- `Directory.Build.props` ensures all .NET projects share the same analyzer versions — no project silently running an older version with different rules

### Negative Consequences

- The initial Husky and lint-staged setup requires all developers to run `npm install` (or equivalent) after cloning to activate the hooks; a developer who skips this step will not have local enforcement until they notice it
- `TreatWarningsAsErrors` for SonarAnalyzer in release builds can surface unexpected build failures when a new analyzer rule is added in a package update; analyzer package updates must be reviewed before merging
- `commitlint` in the commit-msg hook will reject commits that do not follow Conventional Commits; developers unfamiliar with the format will encounter rejection messages and need to amend their first few commits

### Neutral

- Husky is configured via a `prepare` npm script that runs automatically on `npm install`; developers using non-npm tooling (e.g., pnpm, Bun) must ensure the prepare script is also executed
- `svelte-check` reports both type errors and accessibility hints; accessibility hint level can be configured via the `--threshold` flag if it becomes too noisy

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### SonarAnalyzer + StyleCop.Analyzers (chosen)

Both are Roslyn-based, run during `dotnet build`, and integrate with IDEs that support the Roslyn analyzer protocol (VS Code + C# extension, Rider, Visual Studio).

- Good, because violations appear inline in the IDE during development — no separate run step required
- Good, because SonarAnalyzer covers a broad set of quality categories: bugs, vulnerabilities, code smells, complexity
- Good, because StyleCop enforces documentation and member ordering rules that Sonar does not cover
- Bad, because the combined analyzer set can produce a large initial warning volume on a new codebase; a triage session is needed to set the appropriate severity levels

### Roslynator

A comprehensive Roslyn analyser and refactoring pack from JB Roslan.

- Good, because large rule set covering refactoring suggestions beyond what StyleCop covers
- Bad, because significant overlap with SonarAnalyzer; running both creates noise and potential rule conflicts
- Bad, because less commonly used than SonarAnalyzer in enterprise .NET teams; fewer community resources

### CSharpier vs. `dotnet format`

CSharpier is an opinionated formatter (similar to Prettier's philosophy) that reformats entire files with no style configuration. `dotnet format` reads `.editorconfig` and applies those rules.

- `dotnet format` chosen because it respects the team's `.editorconfig` rules and is built into the .NET SDK — no additional tool install required
- CSharpier: good for zero-config formatting; bad because it ignores `.editorconfig` and may produce style that conflicts with StyleCop rules configured there

### Biome vs. ESLint + Prettier

Biome is a single Rust-based tool that covers both linting and formatting for TypeScript/JavaScript.

- Biome good, because a single tool replaces both ESLint and Prettier; fast execution
- Biome bad, because `eslint-plugin-svelte` provides Svelte-specific rules that Biome does not yet support (as of project inception); Svelte component linting would have gaps
- ESLint + Prettier chosen because `eslint-plugin-svelte` and `prettier-plugin-svelte` have mature Svelte support with established rule sets

### Husky + lint-staged vs. lefthook vs. CI-only

- Husky is the most widely adopted git hook manager in the JS ecosystem; integrates with `npm prepare` for automatic installation
- lefthook is a Go-based alternative with better performance for large repos; considered but not chosen as the ecosystem is smaller and the performance difference is negligible at this project's scale
- CI-only enforcement was rejected because it delays feedback: a developer discovers a lint error only after pushing and waiting for CI, rather than immediately on commit

## More Information

- [Conventional Commits specification](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/)
- [commitlint documentation](https://commitlint.js.org/)
- [Husky documentation](https://typicode.github.io/husky/)
- [lint-staged documentation](https://github.com/okonet/lint-staged)
- [SonarAnalyzer for .NET](https://github.com/SonarSource/sonar-dotnet)
- [StyleCop.Analyzers](https://github.com/DotNetAnalyzers/StyleCopAnalyzers)
- [eslint-plugin-svelte](https://sveltejs.github.io/eslint-plugin-svelte/)
- [prettier-plugin-svelte](https://github.com/sveltejs/prettier-plugin-svelte)
